subtopic: SUEZ CANAL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Friday I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs some questions about a caution which the United States government had issued to United States shipping concerning the use of the Suez canal, and the minister replied that he was in touch with Washington and that he hoped to give the house a report at a later date. Is it possible for him to give us that report today?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by a representative of the United States government on this matter last Thursday or Friday to which the hon. gentleman referred
was that ship owners had been advised by the United States government to exercise prudence in the immediate use of the Suez canal. But the United States spokesman added that the state department did not desire to prescribe and prohibit such use at that time. This was interim advice to ship owners which I think might well be accepted by ship owners of other countries. As for Canada, there was no use made of the canal in the 12 months before last July by any ships of Canadian registry.
The question of a more permanent policy with regard to the use of the Suez canal, especially by those countries which are its main users, is now under consideration by the governments concerned, and no decisions have yet been reached by those governments. We are in touch with them on this issue.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
speechtext: A press report in today's Globe and Mail is headed, "West Seen Accepting Nasser Terms on Suez." Can the minister say whether or not that is correct?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, it is not correct, so far as I know, that the governments of the main users of the canal have yet taken any stand in regard to the terms, if you like to call them that, laid down last week by the government of Egypt. That matter is under consideration and, as I have just said, according to our knowledge no final decision has been reached by any government.

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
speechtext: What is the significance of the statement by Nasser in Egypt over the week end that Israeli shipping will not be allowed to use the canal unless and until the Arab refugees are allowed to return to Israel?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUEZ CANAL
speechtext:
I cannot attach any particular significance to that statement, which I have noticed in the press. A statement of that kind, if it were the official position of the Egyptian government, would in our opinion be running counter to resolutions of the United Nations which have previously been passed dealing with free navigation of the Suez canal, and as such certainly would not be approved by us. Also I cannot agree that there is any connection between freedom of navigation of the Suez canal and an appropriate disposition of the refugee problem, important as that problem is.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Saturday, March 30, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdon-nell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last Saturday I was discussing defence expenditures in their relation to the present budget, and I had come rather reluctantly to the conclusion that no matter how heavy the burden of these expenditures might be, it seemed that Canada and the other western powers had no option but to maintain so-called conventional forces as well as nuclear deterrents.
The cost of our defence is heavy. The main estimates already tabled show that for national defence itself $1,700 million is to be spent, for defence production nearly $17 million and for civil defence over $7

million, making a total of $1,746,692,039 or 33.4 per cent of the total government expenditure. There seems no likelihood of any substantial reduction being made in those estimates in the foreseeable future for, in spite of this heavy expenditure, all services lack many essentials, such as arms equipment, transport, both ground and air, buildings and other accommodation. The personnel of our forces is excellent, and it will be recalled that when I returned from Europe last year I praised the efficiency of our troops there; and during the past few months I have seen a good deal of our navy, army and air force in Canada. The men in these forces are splendid, but all units are short of essential armament and equipment. There is just not enough money to go around in the manner it is being distributed at present.
Distribution of the defence dollar among the services is as follows: navy, 15.8 per cent; army 23.2 per cent; air force, 48.5 per cent; mutual aid, 7.55 per cent; research, 3.75 per cent. The remainder is spent on administration. The outlay for R.C.A.F. aircraft and engines alone is $215,603,000, this being within $60 million of the total amount devoted to the navy, and more than half the army's total allotment. If our troops are to obtain the weapons they require to reach the standard of efficiency they deserve, and if the taxpayer is to receive something approaching full value for his defence dollar, there is no room for moneys to be spent on any armament or equipment which is not required for an essential role. All duplication of effort must be removed and interservice rivalries eliminated.
There are so many things the forces need now that we are entering upon the atomic era. Field Marshal Montgomery said last October that in his opinion 50 per cent of all strategic tasks would be performed by missiles in less than ten years, and about 75 per cent of the present type of aircraft used for the support of land armies will have been replaced by nuclear weapons in the hands of land forces. Some of these weapons now urgently required are short-range missiles, guns and howitzers with small atomic heads. There is also the whole field of guided missiles, vertical take-off aircraft, etc., weapons which science has developed and is rapidly making available for those who would use them.
If we are entering the atomic age, as indeed we are, we must approach the problem of defence from a new angle. There must be an honest searching for the truth. It is now time to take a new look at the jobs to be done and the forces and weapons with which to do them. We need to make a most critical
The Budget-Mr. Pearkes investigation to find out the kind of defence we must have. Other countries are reorganizing their forces, and if our organization requires revamping we should not hesitate to take it in hand.
I referred earlier to duplication. Of course there is duplication among the services. For example, both the navy and the R.C.A.F. hunt for submarines. All services have to move their personnel about the country, yet instead of a one-movement staff there are three directorates of transportation. There are so many areas of controversy today brought into existence by the interlocking roles of the three services. Take for instance surface to surface missiles. The army looks upon these as long-range artillery, the air force as pilotless bombers. Helicopters and transport planes are beginning to appear in the army, a sphere of activity belonging until recently to the air force.
The degree of emphasis placed on new aircraft, warning lines and larger airfields, etc. at the expense of development of air portable forces, causes concern amongst the other services. We were told recently that an expenditure of $2 billion would be required to develop a system which would commute the information which would become available through the warning line.
Service rivalries occur annually during the contest over the estimates and the amount of money which is available for each service. In addition there is also duplication between allies. A few years ago we heard a lot about unification. The word is seldom used today, yet in this atomic age national wars are a thing of the past. We cannot do without allies no matter how irksome they may be at times.
Some years ago we embarked on the construction of the CF-100 all-weather long distance fighter. At that time it was the intention to equip regular and auxiliary squadrons with these aircraft. Experience has shown that auxiliary squadrons cannot maintain and navigate these aircraft. The production of the CF-100 therefore has proved more costly, in that we have fewer squadrons to equip. Of course it has always been recognized that intercepter squadrons from the United States air force would augment our fighter squadrons in any battle over Canada. They use a United States built aircraft very similiar to the CF-100. For this and other reasons it has not been possible for Canada to sell abroad her CF-lOO's over and above the requirements of her more limited number of squadrons.
Now we are embarking on the development of the CF-105. The United States is working on a similar type. The missile age is upon us, and the price of a CF-105, if a prototype is

The Budget-Mr. Pearkes accepted, will be many times the cost of the CF-100; it will run into millions. I understand, according to press reports, that the Minister of National Defence stated only on Saturday that this type of aircraft would cost $2 million a plane. That is a moderate estimate, because even the electronic equipment required for this aircraft runs into a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
1 We must keep in mind the fact that fighters are of diminishing value now as a deterrent. -In the United Kingdom the select committee -on the estimates was called upon to ascertain whether value has been, and is being, obtained for the large sums of money voted for the Supply of aircraft. Their report reviewed the changing military and economic situation since world war II, and related this to the decisions to order and produce particular aircraft at *various times. The conclusions and recommendations of this committee are worthy of careful study. The first conclusion reads as follows:
Although understandable in the economic circumstances of the time, the money spent on developing aircraft which were unsuccessful in competition and which therefore never went into production, seems excessive, and the system itself one which should not be resorted to in other fields, such as missiles or equipment, without its objectionable features being fully taken into account.
With the advent of the atomic and missile era upon us, we must ourselves carry out a critical examination of each new project originating either with a service department or a research establishment, in order to ascertain its effect upon our aircraft construction industry. The relative value of production from original designs, buying direct from another allied country, or building in Canada from foreign designs under a licence from the designer must be weighed in the balance.
On March 11 the Minister of Defence Production advised that a tentative agreement had been entered into with the de Havilland company for an advance of $2,500,000 to promote the development of an army transport plane referred to as the Caribou. In view of the fact that the United States army is also interested in this type of aircraft, this deal would seem to indicate a degree of co-operation between Canada and the United States not so noticeable heretofore. I have advocated in this house over and over again that our land forces should be airborne or air-transportable, but today a suitable aircraft is not available.
I have mentioned this field of aircraft development mainly because great sums of money are involved, and because of the complexity of the problem. But in many other fields great changes are pending; that is, if we are to have modern defence forces. There
	i i

are many of these interservice problems connected with the future upon which decisions cannot be given without the most careful and searching review. The Minister of National Defence said on March 12, in answer to a question about streamlining our forces, that we are "constantly studying the condition and strength of our forces, and, keeping in mind all the relevant factors, we are making changes as changes appear to be warranted." The minister added, "As a matter of fact, I have announced changes in the house on one or two occasions recently."
These changes have, of course, been of a minor nature, and have the appearance of being introduced to meet some immediate problem rather than as part of an over-all pattern. It is all very well for the minister to say that all relevant factors are being kept in mind, but the means for future planning are hardly available to him. He must rely upon advice from his service chiefs. These are excellent men; I know them all personally. They are all very busy men immersed in the day to day questions affecting their own service. They have little time to work out a broad plan to meet future requirements. Then again, there are certain inherent difficulties in the way of the devising of an over-all defence organization by the chiefs of staff.
Each is the head of a military service and feels responsible for the state of readiness and the morale of its personnel. He instinctively resents any encroachment upon the prerogatives of his service and his own lifetime loyalties. Chiefs of staff hold their appointments for relatively short periods, and assume office at different times. Therefore there is no continuity of planning.
Because these interservice battle areas exist, it must not be assumed that each chief of staff is an inflexible individual. I know the contrary to be the fact. However, each has grown up in the traditions of his particular service, and each no doubt feels that in addition to his broader responsibilities as a member of the joint chiefs of staff committee he has an individual responsibility to his own service.
We have seen in the past that it has been necessary for other countries to set up independent inquiries, not composed of Colonel Blimps nor of members of parliament, but of high judicial personnel who are capable of hearing and interpreting evidence. I refer to such committees as the Esher committee which was formed in Great Britain at the beginning of this century, the result of whose deliberations was the complete overhaul of the war office and an adjustment of duties as between the royal navy and the army of the

United Kingdom. I do not say it would be possible for us to set up a committee with any thought of reducing over-all expenditure, but I feel it is essential that there must be long-term planning in order that we may get full value from the defence dollar which is voted, and also that the services themselves may get the types of equipment which it is so essential for them to have and which they do not have at the present time.
Because a lot of service controversy results from competition, various measures have been suggested to solve the problem. The idea of a single service has been advanced; our tri-service colleges have proved a successful experiment in this direction. Perhaps Canada is in a position to experiment further in that direction. Alternatively there is the possibility of a unified command. A step in that direction would be to make the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee the chief of staff of the defence forces. Anyhow, every senior officer to whom one speaks stresses the need for closer integration among the services.
With two great power groups, west and east, each able to destroy each other with the weapons science has produced, we cannot permit a situation to develop which would provide the opportunity for these powers to commit national suicide. Our aim must be peace; but as things stand today it seems that the best way to secure peace is through strength, and' in co-operation with other nations having similar views. This means that for the foreseeable future we must continue to maintain our defence force at a high standard of efficiency and in a state of readiness to meet an emergency. They cannot meet an emergency, they cannot be efficient, if they are not given the essential weapons.
The same thing applies not only to the regular but also to the reserve forces of the country. Today our Canadian militia has no clearly defined role. Its role and organization are in no way related to those of the regular forces or to anything it might conceivably be called upon to carry out. It is still based on the old system of divisional organization which, as I explained on Saturday, is now a thing of the past.
Our civil defence system is far from efficient. It has comparatively little money devoted to it. If there is a danger of Canada being used as an air pathway to the United States, then there is a grave danger that bombs may fall on this land. Therefore civil defence is required. We have spent time and money in order to secure the report of the Gordon commission, which is based on the assumption that there will be no war for
The Budget-Mr. Poulin 20 years, and has planned the economic development of Canada with that in mind. It seems to me that consideration might well be given to establishing some commission which, having in mind the long-term planning, would see what could be done to ensure that there is no war in the next 20 years.
As I have already stated, in my opinion the only assurance that can be given is through strength. Therefore we must see to it that the available money is used to the very best advantage, and that there is some means by which long-term planning can be carried out. That means does not exist today. That is my feeling on this subject. We are spending a lot of money on national defence and will have to continue to spend a lot of money. We have fine forces, but they are lacking in modern equipment. Therefore in order to provide them with the equipment and arms they need it is essential that all duplication between services and between allies be eliminated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday evening, when I had to interrupt my remarks so that this house could proceed with the vote in accordance with the rules, I was dealing with the position of the sugar industry in Beauce county. I was asking the government to restore the subsidy for the replacement of sap-pails, and I added that a price support for the sale of maple products should be established. I had to stop right in the middle of a sentence which I am going to repeat to-day, in order to connect last Thursday's remarks with those I am going to make now.
I understand from the contents of a letter the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) wrote to me, in answer to a request I had made, that the officials of his department were considering the possibility of resorting to the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act in an attempt to reach a financially acceptable arrangement in respect of the sale of maple products.
I know that this act was resorted to in some cases, particularly for the sale of turkeys in the county of Dorchester, for instance, to help producers out of their difficulties arising from a slump in the marketing of their product. I am not sure, however, that the case of the sugar producers who are not grouped as co-operatives-and there are still too many of them-could be solved in this way. Yet they should get the same help as the others. I do hope the issue will be considered quickly and effectively and that, if my humble suggestions prove impracticable,

The Budget-Mr. Poulin our experts will come up with other and sounder ones to solve these very important issues.
As a matter oi fact, maple sugar producers would not be the only ones to benefit from special assistance legislation, for by now, the wheat, butter, bacon, egg, apple, fish and turkey producers are in the same position. In view of the fact that the federal government has entered the field of production, it would be all the more justified in entering the field of marketing, since a considerable percentage of this produce in particular is meant for export and sale across the border.
On the other hand, there is every reason to believe, as I pointed out last year to the producers of Beauce county, that the new marketing office legislation in the province of Quebec will be able to help in this respect, but some might also wonder about its powers with regard to fixing a price for a product that is to be sold outside the country.
A few years ago I was instrumental, along with some others, in getting an inquiry and report made under the Combines Investigation Act, on the sale price of maple products. I am happy to say that some good work has been done. On several occasions, during two or three years, I personally called on the director of investigation; I always found a kind welcome, and all cases I submitted, with adequate indications and details, were seriously looked into. So there is no lack of good will, and I am sure that if the minister were to give instructions to do so an objective research would be made. That is why I am anxious for the Minister of Agriculture to grant my request, and I can assure him that the whole county of Beauce will be grateful to him for it.
On January 10 last the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Laflamme) put before the house the need for decentralization of administration as far as unemployment insurance is concerned and asked for a larger number of offices, so that the unemployed would not have to travel long distances at their own expense to submit their claims.
I am happy to agree with that proposal. In Beauce county, for example, the unemployed often have to travel some 25 or 30 miles to the local office. And when they get there, they often find officials who would be only too glad to help them but are swamped with work due to the great number of people who have to go to that office. In these circumstances the employee does not have the time to give the worker all the explanations he would need to properly understand his own


case. As a matter of fact, I do not know what the majority of the members of this house think about it, but I know that, as far as I am concerned, I have a lot of trouble finding my way through that mess of regulations and sometimes I have to look for a long time before coming across the one that fits my particular case. Small farmers and lumber-jacks cannot make head or tail of it. The claimant, especially when he is turned down, should be able to understand why his claim is disallowed. Otherwise he goes away grumbling, and not without cause. But, in those cases which it is often quite difficult to straighten out, how can we expect the employee who is continuously hustled and dazed by all that crowding and overwork to take the time to give his client the elaborate explanations he would need?
I do not blame the employees, far from it; they are doing all they can under conditions which are often hopeless. Nor do I blame the worker, the lumber-jack or the small farmer. After all we cannot ask them to get a university degree so that they may be able to understand the legislation. I put the blame on the organization.
Quite often, precisely because he did not understand the explanations and is not satisfied, the claimant feels he should make a second trip to the office for further explanations. This of course means additional expenses, often to no good purpose because the employee, who is getting more and more overworked, is still unable to give the client all the time that would be required in the circumstances. And the more unsatisfied claimants you get, the more often you see them go back to the office, where the crowding gets worse, the harder it is to clear up each case and the greater the dissatisfaction of all concerned. It becomes sort of a lasting vicious circle, with some acute phases at certain times of the year.
I am convinced that the administration of an unemployment insurance office is much more difficult in the country than in a city. At least it is so in the region I represent. Why? Because more often there than elsewhere, you meet particular classes of wage earners who come under a category of insurable employment governed by extremely complicated regulations.
In my humble opinion, there should be more offices. This would cut down expenses considerably for the claimants; it would make it easier for them to call at the office, and in the

second place it would relieve the crowding and make it easier for the office employee to give the unemployed all explanations necessary to properly understand his case, which would make for a satisfied client, even when his claim had to be turned down. Besides, I am quite sure that fewer claims would be rejected if the employees could take the time to make a more thorough study of each particular case.
I may add that the unemployment commission experts should again consider the case of the small farmers who are working for wages outside their farm, as well as the case of the bush workers. Some important changes should certainly be made in those two categories. I think I can grasp the meaning of the words: off-season, small income, main occupation and various others. Yet, I shall never understand why a farmer who, in one or two years, has accumulated as many contributions as a city worker, should not get the same benefit. If he has worked long enough outside his farm to accumulate the minimum payments that are required of a worker, his farm necessarily becomes a secondary matter and his salaried employment is his main job. Let him therefore be treated accordingly.
Despite its complexity the case of fishermen was settled by the commission in a sound and practical way. If the same efficiency and intelligence is put to work in the case of the small farmer, everybody will be satisfied. As to the bush workers in my area, they very often ask me if the government will manage to enter into a mutual agreement with certain American States with regard to an exchange of unemployment benefits. There are, indeed, in the county of Beauce, a great many bush workers who are employed in Maine, and some also in New Hampshire. If I understand the position rightly, these are the only two states that have no agreement with Canada as yet.
I know that, on January 15 last, the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), stated in answer to a question on the orders of the day, that there had been some progress in these agreement negotiations. I want to thank him, in the name of our bush workers, for the effort he is making in this field, and I also ask him to pursue this effort so as to hasten matters, if possible, as he may be assured that the day this happy result is reached, he will have rendered a considerable service to a whole category of workers who are numerous and significant throughout the country, more particularly in my county of Beauce.
The Budget-Mr. Poulin
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to add a few words more particularly connected with the budget speech of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris).
I readily admit that better conditions now exist at the national level, at least as far as the position of the farmer is concerned. However, we have to recognize that this favourable change is mainly noticeable in western Canada. As a matter of fact, I cannot see, for instance, in what respect the lot of the Beauce farmer has advanced. The price of animals and butcher's meat has not improved at the producer's level, nor has the price of bacon, butter, eggs or maple sugar. About the only improvement has been in the price of wood. And if we compare the rise in the price index for goods and services bought by farmers, we are forced to the conclusion that the position is worse than it has been for the past few years, and it certainly is at least far from being as interesting as in 1951 and 1952.
What of the price of farm implements, feed and labour? The agricultural costs index, which I was mentioning a moment ago, has gone from 224.5 in 1955 to 229.4 in 1956.
As far as manual workers are concerned, I must admit that the skilled worker gets good wages, but the unskilled labourer is still in a most difficult position, the increase in the cost of living having quickly wiped out the increase in salary scales. The position of office workers, store clerks or industrial workers is hardly better, for the same reason.
And what of the father of a large family?
I think that one should be in intimate contact with these people and have occasion to go into their homes to be able to judge with any accuracy at all what their situation is. Prices are constantly going up. Bread, milk, medicine, shoes, clothing, everything is going up. I wonder if the hon. Minister of Finance was taking himself seriously when he granted a $1.00 a month increase to a certain limited number of children already in receipt of family allowances, but not to all, as it might be well to remember at this point. A large number of fathers and mothers will wonder whether they have not been having nightmares when they find out that not one child in the 6, 7, 8 and 9 year group or in the 13, 14, 15 and 16 year group will receive one solitary cent increase in family allowances. Using as a basis the figures provided by the Minister of Finance,

The Budget-Mr. Poulin it is not surprising then to find that families in receipt of family allowances will benefit from an average increase of no more than $16.80 a year, that is $1.40 per month. If the thousands of taxpayers from the constituency of Beauce who have signed and forwarded requests to me demanding an increase in family allowances, and even requesting the amount to be doubled, are satisfied with this result, I will say to them that there must be only one explanation for this and it is because they are easily satisfied, or else are used to getting by on mighty little. They asked for a 100 per cent increase. A 50 per cent increase might have been acceptable, but what they have received is an increase of approximately 10.5 per cent.
Another excellent way to help the low income groups of taxpayers would have been to reduce the sales tax, without touching, of course, the 2 per cent which is used to set up the old age pension fund. I have made that suggestion more than once since I have been in this house. According to the budget speech, under this heading, fiscal revenues for 1956-57 have been $725 millions, a very tidy sum indeed.
A noteworthy fact is that, of all sources of indirect taxation, this is by far the most productive; in fact, among all direct and indirect taxes it ranks third, immediately after individual income tax and corporation income tax. Well, who is paying this 10 percent tax? The consumer, of course. And who is the consumer? It is everybody, no doubt, but including the poor chap who cannot even afford to pay income tax, it is the disabled, the blind, the needy mother, the subsidized settler, the old aged pensioner, all people who cannot fully provide for themselves and have to rely on the government which takes back with one hand part of what it gives with the other. But the real consumer is, above all, the head of the family; and the bigger his family the heavier his burden. As far as the head of a large family is concerned, exemptions and compensations in proportion to the number of children will never restore a fair and equitable balance, as long as the government does not radically reduce the rate of that sales tax, a tax which nobody sees but which is paid by everyone and which will, this year, deprive the consumer of $751 million, a tax which affects the small taxpayer as well as the wealthy and often more, precisely on account of his situation as head of the family. Instead of appropriating a sum of $100 million for the Canadian Council of Arts the government could have used that money to reduce the sales tax.

The provinces have the duty and the power to deal with the cultural problem, and they could do it much better than the central government if only that government had left them the necessary sources of revenue.
I wish to add that the government should have raised to $2,000 and $3,000 the income tax basic exemption for bachelors and married people respectively. That too is a request I have made on many occasions in the last few years. I will leave it at that.
In conclusion may I say that if I felt it my duty, last year, to show my confidence in the government by voting in favour of the Minister of Finance's budget, this year, for the reasons I have just given as well as for others, I feel that I must vote against the government.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to spend a great deal of time on the budget as such. There is, of course, not too much in it on which to spend time. I intend, rather, to deal with some of its implications and omissions.
The budget is characterized by increased social security benefits and scattered tax concessions, spread as thinly as possible in order to give a very small amount of help to the greatest number of people without cutting too much into the minister's large surplus. It is obviously a pre-election budget, in which the Minister of Finance has tried to give the illusion that the government is deeply concerned about the welfare of our less well off citizens, thereby providing the opportunity for Liberal candidates to tell their electors about the gifts, so-called, which the government has given them.
This has been Liberal strategy during the last three elections, and evidently it is to be the basis of their campaign this year. I do not think it will be as successful as it has been in the past, because an increasing number of our people have come to realize that the government can give them nothing; it merely returns to them a certain proportion of the money it has previously taken out of their pockets by taxation. The increase in the old age pension is miserly. I have no doubt that some of the recipients would not agree with this statement. I am sure, for example, the Prime Minister believes the increase is adequate. I am quite sure both the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture believe the increase is adequate. I would agree with them that it is adequate so far as they are concerned, because they do not need it at all. But it is not adequate for

those who are wholly or almost wholly dependent upon it. The increase in the cost of living has left these people in a hopeless situation, in which they cannot live at a decent level. The increase of $6 per month is not enough to correct the situation.
The same thing, of course, applies to those on old age assistance and those who are blind. It is this considerable segment of our population who desperately need help, and it is this segment who do not get help to any great extent from this budget. I was particularly sorry, Mr. Speaker, to find that the special guidance allowance, without a means test, requested by the blind was not provided in this budget. I would hope the Minister of Finance might still provide for it at this session. The cost to the treasury of a guiding or special blindness allowance would not be too great and these, the most seriously handicapped of our citizens, are surely entitled to this small special consideration.
I was glad to see that there were some increases in benefits for the veterans in this budget. However, once again they fall far short of what was requested by the Legion and other veterans organizations, and what is necessary to compensate the veterans for the increases which have taken place in the cost of living. The veterans organizations of this country asked for a 33J per cent increase in pensions, but the budget provides for an increase varying from nothing for a single man on war veterans allowance to a maximum increase of 20 per cent for a single man on full disability pension.
These meagre increases allowed to the war pensioner puts him in a far worse relative position than he was in away back immediately after the first great war. In the February, 1957, issue of the publication put out by the Canadian Legion, called the Legionary, there is a chart which shows the relative position of the 100 per cent single disability pensioner, back in 1920, at the time this was put out before the introduction of the budget, and the position the pensioner is in at the present time until the increase provided for becomes effective.
In 1920 the single man on full pension received $900. The theory when these pensions were put into effect was that the rate of pension would be the same as the income a labourer would receive and, as a matter of fact, the pensions at that time were comparable. At that same time, in 1920, for example, a civil service cleaner and helper received exactly the same amount, $900, and the pensioner and the common labourer were on a par.
The Budget-Mr. Harkness
At the present time we have this situation. A single man receives $1,500 a year. The civil service cleaner and helper, who is taken merely as an example, receives $2,760 a year. In other words, his position has become nearly twice as good as that of the single man on full disability pension.
What the figures produced by the Legioii indicate is that after this budget goes into effect a single man will receive a total of $1,800 a year, just under two-thirds of what the cleaner and helper receives, or in other words two-thirds of what the ordinary common labourer is able to receive and does receive at the present time in our economy. It is, I think, a very clear indication to what extent the pensioner has suffered from inflation, and it indicates also very clearly the refusal of this government to recognize the debt owed by the country to these men and the government's failure to maintain the level of pensions which was established back at the end of the first world war by a Conservative government.
I call upon the Minister of Finance and the government to restore veterans pensions to their original position in purchasing power and relative to civilian wages. Until this is done I think it is futile for government speakers, as they have done so frequently in the past, to go about this country boasting that our treatment of our veterans and returned men is the best of any country in the world.
The largest section of our people, namely the average householder and his wife, are the very people for which this government does practically nothing. The abolition of the sales tax on tea, coffee, pickles and a few other items does, of course, affect this average householder and his family and grants him an infinitesimal amount of relief. Similarly, depending on the number of children he has] the amount he will receive of $1, $2, $3 a month, because of the increase in family allowances, provides an infinitesimal measure of relief and help to him. The increase in children's allowances is sufficient to buy five additional quarts of milk per child, and that is all.
Perhaps the person who has been hit as hard as anyone in this country by the rise in the cost of living and the increases in prices that we have had is the average householder, the man on $3,000-odd a year, or something in that neighbourhood. In other words the average consumer is the forgotten man. He is the forgotten man in this budget; he is the forgotten man generally as far as the government is concerned.	t

The Budget-Mr. Harkness
I should like to turn to another matter, Mr. Speaker. One of the notable omissions in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance is any review of the present situation in regard to housing construction, or any measures designed to improve it. During the latter part of the 1956 session we had many indications that the tight money policy of the government was having, and was likely to have, very serious effects on the housing industry. The replies of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works to inquiries made in this house last summer, and again throughout this session, as to what measures were contemplated to prevent a great decline in house building were really nothing more than a sort of soothing syrup. They reiterated statements that house building was not declining to begin with, and later, when the fact that it was declining became inescapable, their statements were that the decline was not serious and that the situation would correct itself shortly.
The fact that all these statements we have had were incorrect is shown up quite conclusively by a publication which I received just a few days ago entitled, "Canadian Housing Statistics", put out by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, dated March, 1957. It shows that the decline in housing starts has indeed been very serious. If we look at page 7 we find the statistics in regard to this. In the 'last quarter of 1955 the total number of house starts was 32,069. In the last quarter of 1956 the total number was 23,874, or a decline of 8,195 in the actual number of houses started in those three months.
When we look at the right hand side of the statistics provided in this same table, which gives the annual rate of decrease, the seriousness of the situation shows up even more definitely. In the last quarter of 1955 the rate of dwelling starts was 142,700; in the last quarter of 1956 the rate was only 106,200. Now, this is the rate; they were started at that rate. I have given the annual figures before. In other words there is a decline in the annual rate of construction of 36,500 houses, a very large number of houses. Similarly, the decline in the annual number of houses constructed in those two comparative quarters of 1955 and 1956 is at a percentage rate of 25.5.
These figures, I think, show quite clearly that we have had what anyone, except this government, would consider a very serious decline in house building. That presents us, of course, with a situation to which I think the government, the house and the country need to pay particular and serious attention. However, Mr. Speaker, I have reason to
IMr. Harkness.]
believe that the situation in this year of 1957 is much worse than that shown by the figures up to the end of 1956.
I have a few statistics and opinions of builders in various parts of Canada to back up this statement. For example, on February 20 of this year at Windsor, Ontario-

Well, on February 20 this year in the minister's city of Windsor, Ontario, only 18 National Housing Act loans had been processed since the beginning of the year, compared with several hundred at the same date last year, 1956.
Last year in Windsor at the same date approximately 1,600 N.H.A. loans were made available to people to build houses, whereas on February 20 this year, although the exact number was not available, it was estimated that there would not be any more than 200 at the most. That is some indication of the seriousness of the housing situation in Windsor. My information is that no loans at all were available in Newfoundland at the middle of February this year, and very few were available in the maritimes generally.
The statistics concerning housing in my own city of Calgary appear on page 10 of this report, and I find them extremely interesting. In 1955 a total of 3,129 houses were started, and in 1956 a total of 3,742 were started. This represents a considerable increase, and is contrary to the general trend across the country. From reading the statistics one would gather the impression that the housing picture in Calgary is quite bright, but as a matter of fact the picture given by the statistics is quite misleading with relation to the period we are now in.
The sum total of N.H.A. loans expected to be available in Calgary for the entire year, as estimated at February 15, was only 450. There was a possibility that a reallocation of funds from other areas might increase this total slightly, but little hope was offered that this would improve the situation to any marked degree. There was also available in Calgary as at the middle of February from 300 to 400 conventional loans, some of them with interest rates as high as 7 per cent per annum. If you add the limited number of houses which will be built by individuals under their own financing arrangements it develops that unless something is done to improve matters the total number of houses

built in Calgary this year will be decreased to 1,100 or 1,200 as compared with the 3,742 built last year. In other words less than one-third of the number constructed last year will be built in 1957.
This estimate of the total number of houses likely to be built in Calgary this year unless steps are taken is confirmed by the action of the Calgary city commissioners in curtailing their land expansion program by over 50 per cent. The total number of lots that were planned to be ready for use this year in Calgary was approximately 4,000 and about 3,500 lots were expected to be built on. This figure has now been cut back to 1,500 lots which will be made available in 1957, and the Calgary builders feel this will be more than adequate for the building which will be done there this year.
This presents a picture which is much more serious than the figures for 1956 and previous years would indicate, and the situation is much more serious than the government will admit. It is one that calls for immediate and definite action on the part of the government to ensure that funds are available for the housing that our rapidly increasing population needs.
There are of course several things that might be done in order to ease this situation, and I would suggest two. The first is direct lending on the part of the government or its agencies. A certain amount of this has been done in the past, but it presents various difficulties especially for prospective home owners and builders, who find it difficult to make adequate use of such funds because of the restrictions imposed on them and because of the percentage of the loan which is allowed as against the total cost of the house. However, it is a course which may have to be resorted to if mortgage money is not available otherwise, and one which the government should resort to if no other means can be found to correct the situation which has developed.
The second course of action I would suggest is the institution of a system of buying up loans and brokeraging them out to sources of money which ordinarily do not or cannot readily take up housing loans. Such a system exists in the United States under the nickname "Fanny May". It is carried on through the federal national mortgage association, which I understand has purchased an average of about $22 million worth of mortgages a week for the last two or three years and then sold them to other investors. I believe the system is working very well. At the middle of January last the association had only $43,500,000 of mortgages on hand for sale in spite of the billions they have handled.
The Budget-Mr. J. A. Power
There are, of course, other ways of improving what is rapidly developing into a dangerous situation, but this government does nothing about it except to issue soothing and misleading statements. Before this session is ended the house and the country are entitled to a statement by the Minister of Public Works as to what the situation is at the present time, and what steps will be taken to ensure the continuance of home construction on an adequate scale.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Power (Si. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my word of praise to the Minister of Finance for the excellent budget he has produced this year. Despite what has been said here about overtaxation or about tax receipts outdistancing government expenditure, a surplus on the year's operations is a much more comforting thing than a deficit.
1 suppose in one sense government finan-ing is like personal financing. The man who allows his annual spending to exceed his income has to expect real trouble some day. Importunate creditors are equally tough at either level. Mr. Micawber expressed it well after a lifetime of deficit financing when he said that saving or overspending ten shillings a year constituted the difference between happiness and misery. Starting a new financial year, the government is able to apply some of last year's surplus to tax reductions and to significant increases in social benefits.
Living costs in Newfoundland are affected to a great extent by freight costs. The bulk of food and other commodities forming part of ordinary family consumption in Newfoundland are purchased, in the main, west of the maritime provinces. It is obvious that freight charges are a big factor in the ultimate cost to the consumer. It is encouraging to see that there is a substantial increase in the freight subvention on goods moving out of Newfoundland into other parts of Canada, though it must be admitted that this subvention increase will not have nearly the same effect on the Newfoundland economy as an increase in freight subventions moving in the other direction.
It is encouraging to note that the government intends to make an immediate review of all transportation in the Atlantic region, and that it is sympathetic toward further substantial improvements in the freight rate picture.
Today is the eighth anniversary of the union of Newfoundland with Canada. 1 do not think any one can deny that the economic position of the average Newfoundlander is much better today than it was eight years ago.
[DOT]2922

The Budget-Mr. J. A. Power Quite apart from the effect of really substantial payments in the various forms of social welfare benefits, Newfoundland has profited from the ordinary operations of a number of federal departments and agencies there. Canadian National Railways has spent large capital sums in the improvement of railway and Shipping facilities. The Department of Public Works has done a lot-more, I think, than is generally realized-in building up dock and harbour facilities, even in the very smallest fishing settlements. I can think of a number of places in St. John's West where construction of a breakwater or a wharf has had the effect of materially lengthening the fishing season and of allowing cheaper entry of some of the heavier commodities.
The port of St. John's is the oldest in North America. It was extensively used by the fishing fleets of all the maritime European nations at the time that Sir Humphrey Gilbert took possession of Newfoundland in the name of 'the first Elizabeth. It is a historical fact that the port was the centre of the English western Atlantic fishing industry long before that date, and indeed, from only a few years after John Cabot's first voyage in 1497.
From the beginning, St. John's has been, and still is, the commercial centre of the island. The Department of Transport has realized this fact and is now engaged in an extensive survey of the harbour with a view to the construction of harbour works toward its improvement and more economic utilization. There is a strong feeling in St. John's that the port should be made a national harbour and come under the management of the national harbours board. The value of this [DOT]secure port was more than evident during the two world wars when it gave sure refuge to large convoys of merchant ships and was used as a point for the assembly of these fleets to the British Isles.
In addition to the survey of the harbour now under way, there is strong reason to believe that this will lead to the construction of a million dollar project by the Department of Transport to house the marine agencies now in existence there, including docking facilities for a large ship, now under construction, to to used for the purpose of placing and servicing buoys and other aids to navigation.
The budget forecasts aid in power development in flic Atlantic region, particularly in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I would like to draw the attention of the government to the vast hydro electric power potential in Newfoundland. Newfoundland is the ninth of the provinces in population, the seventh in [DOT]area and the fourth or fifth in water power. The provincial government, through the British and Newfoundland corporation, has

undertaken wide surveys of the water resources in Labrador, assisted in this regard by a very thorough mapping project done by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. In Sweden, hydro-electric power has been carried economically for a distance of over 600 miles. Surely it is within the bounds of possibility that future research should increase this distance to the extent that power developed on the Hamilton river in Labrador could be put into use in the central part of Canada at a price that should allow it to compete with power developed from coal, natural gas or atomic energy.
As I mentioned earlier, today is the eighth anniversary of the union and in this connection I would like to draw the attention of the house to term 29 of the terms of union. Term 29 deals with a projected review of the financial position of Newfoundland after her entry into confederation. It reads: In view of the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada, the government of Canada will appoint a royal commission within eight years from the date of union to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
To give effect to this term the government recently established a royal commission consisting of the Chief Justice of New Brunswick as chairman, and the Chief Justice of Newfoundland and Mr. John Deutsch of the staff of the University of British Columbia, and a former senior civil servant, as additional members. Public comment in Newfoundland has expressed full confidence in the make-up of the commission. About two years ago the provincial government set up a committee to make a study of the financial position of the province and to present the Newfoundland case to the commission. This committee has functioned continuously since then and I understand has recently completed its task. People in Newfoundland are hopeful that the report of the commission will result in considerably increased financial aid from the treasurer to the government of the province.
One too evident fact is that the province, with an area of 150,000 square miles and a population of only 415,000, requires much larger per capita sums for the provision of ordinary public services than does a province with a more concentrated population. To illustrate this, the trans-Canada highway in

Newfoundland runs for a distance of 610 miles. Provision of the provincial share of the cost of construction bears to a much greater extent on the individual Newfoundland taxpayer than the provincial share of the cost in any other province, although population figures show that the inclusion of Newfoundland in the larger picture did not bring about what a great many people feared. It was thought that with the removal of immigration barriers consequent upon the union large numbers of Newfoundlanders would take advantage of this to migrate to other parts of Canada. The fact is that our population has increased by nearly 100,000 since union and the figures of the census taken last year show that Newfoundland's increase of population in the preceding five years was almost exactly equal to the rate of population growth of Canada as a whole.
The union with Newfoundland has brought to Canada a province with immeasurable wealth in resources of land and sea, and the people of the new province are entitled to expect that they will have every just assistance in converting these potentials into added wealth for our nation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to discuss what I think is a very important matter having to do with the administration of the Department of Agriculture. I was very happy, sir, to see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has returned from his sojourn in western Canada. I presume it is well-known he was out there using political haywire to mend political fences in that province; but I think he will find that hay-wire or any other Liberal wire will not do much good in that province for the Liberal party from now on.
It is well known in this chamber that last year there was an important discussion which was, I think, of great public importance.
Last week I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) if it would be possible to give the assurance that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture would be discussed by the house before the end of the session. Because no assurance was given and the fact that the session is drawing to a close, I want to bring this very important matter to the attention of the house at this time. I refer, of course, to the compensation of over $100,000 paid by the Department of Agriculture for 674 sheep slaughtered last year. To whom was the $100,000 paid? It was paid to Mr. P. J. Rock, a well-known breeder and one of the most prominent Liberal supporters in Alberta. The average price paid was $150 per sheep.

Never until last year had such compensation been paid for the destruction of sheep. I have figures here as to the numbers slaughtered and average amounts paid under the compensation policy. In 1945-46, 102 sheep were destroyed with an average payment of $20 each. In 1951-52, 65 sheep were destroyed with an average payment of $34 each. In 1952-53 there were 11 sheep destroyed with an average payment of $47 each and finally, in 1954-55 there were 108 sheep destroyed with an average payment of $75 each.
But last year the minister came before the house and could not give us any substantial reason why he should take over $100,000 out of the public funds and pay it to one individual. He tried to appear so naive as to leave the impression that he was not aware that this man was a Liberal supporter and perhaps one of the greatest Liberal supporters in the province of Alberta. From examining last year's records it appears that the truth of the matter is that many lambs were born after the disease was diagnosed in this flock, and rumours persist that some of these sheep have not been destroyed. Rumours persist that substitutions have been made and also that some of the sheep were moved from P. J. Rock's flock to a farm in Manitoba. I am inclined to believe these rumours. In going through Hansard of last year I find that on July 13,1956, as found at page 5960, the Minister of Agriculture was asked a question and gave the following answer:
Mr. Rock in 1955-56 had 674 sheep slaughtered and they were all registered. There is not any question about them being slaughtered or of their being substitutions. The compensation paid was $100,050.
The hon. member for Battle River-Cam-rose (Mr. Smith) then said to the minister:
I would like to have some assurance from the minister before we end this discussion that the registrations of these purebred animals have been turned in to the department. Have they been turned over?
The minister replied:
Yes, they were all turned in to the department.
Then, at page 5962 I find that the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton) asked this question of the minister:
I should like to know if the meat was used when these sheep were slaughtered, and who got the value of the meat.
The minister replied:	"They were all
buried." The hon. member for Brant-Haldimand then said:
It has been suggested that there were some substitutions made in this flock before the date the animals were slaughtered and buried.

The minister replied: "They had all been checked." As found at page 5963, the minister went on to say:
Right from the time the disease was diagnosed the ear tag numbers were taken.
I comment here that if that is the case and the information given by the minister is true there should be metal tags on the carcasses of these buried animals. At page 5964 the minister went on to say:
The ear tag numbers are all here, as my hon. friend knows. Those sheep were all registered, and the ear tag numbers were all known here, no matter when they were sold. The transfers are all registered.
I comment here that the minister should then have the actual registrations. If the minister will not take action to clear up this matter it is a certainty that rumours will persist that some skulduggery has taken place involving the misappropriation of public funds. Not only is $100,000 in public money a very questionable sum to pay for 674 sheep, many of which were lambs, but the minister's actions and responsibilities with regard to making sure that there were no substitutions are also before the bar of public opinion. The minister was using public funds and I say that action should be taken by the minister to clear up the matter.
I should like to make several suggestions. First, a special investigating committee of the house should be established to investigate thoroughly everything connected with this matter. Second, the minister should table in the house immediately the 674 registrations. I do not believe that the minister can produce the registrations for all these sheep. The minister has said the registrations are in the hands of his department. I challenge him to produce them. While I do not believe the minister can produce the actual registration certificates, even if he does the air will not be cleared of the suggestion of skulduggery. Third, the minister should be able to table all the correspondence between government officials, P. J. Rock and the appraisers to show, among other things, the date on which the first inspection of the flock was made and the date on which the flock became subject to scrapie.
The minister has stated that the sheep were buried, and in order to clear the minister I say that in the fourth place the carcasses of the sheep should be exhumed and examined to see if the metal ear tags are on them corresponding with the certificates which the minister claims are in the possession of his department. I say that when and only when the minister is prepared to go this far can he be cleared of the persistent rumours that substitutions have been made with regard to these sheep.


Members of the house who are familiar with the purebred livestock business know that a metal tag as well as an India ink tattoo is placed on the ear of every purebred animal. Together with the tag of the health of animals branch, there may be a metal tag used by the owner for the purpose of identifying each animal. I think I have indicated to the minister and to the house that it rests with the Minister of Agriculture to clear the air regarding the allegations I am making with reference to the persistent rumours that there has been skulduggery in respect of this huge payment to one individual. I think the wool has been pulled over people's eyes and it is up to the minister to follow the suggestions I have indicated.
Fifty dollars a head was a very high price for these sheep.

This man was paid $150 for each sheep. I agree with the hon. member that $50 would probably be a fair and reasonable price, but in this case the minister saw fit to bring in appraisers and pay the amount of $150 for each sheep. After what I have said I think this matter rests with the Minister of Agriculture. There have been persistent rumours that some of these sheep have been removed to a Manitoba farm. I do not think it rests with any member of the house to go any farther than I have done. It is now up to the minister to clear the air so that he can face the bar of public opinion.
I am interested in one or two other matters that I should like to bring to the attention of the house this afternoon. First, it will be recalled that we of this party have asked for a better deal for our older citizens. I refer to the request we have made that the old age pension be increased to $75. In my opinion that would be a fair amount to pay them and certainly would be commensurate with our gross national product.

That is perfectly all right. I am amazed at the niggardly increase that was granted. I have also noticed an article in the Leader-Post

stating that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) had said that a figure of $75 was not realistic.
To him as the leader of the official opposition party I want to say that in my books neither is the figure of $46 for our older people realistic, nor is it realistic to expect them to live on it in decency and security with the cost of living as it is today. Therefore I am rather amazed that the Progressive Conservative leader should come out and say that the figure of $75 is not realistic. I am even more interested when the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) said a few moments ago with respect to the pensions for veterans that he and his party-and I believe he was speaking for his party as well as for himself-wanted an increase over the $150 now paid to our war veterans. I go along with him, as I still think that this is not adequate. However when you compare that figure with the $900 which we of the CCF are asking for our old age pensioners, I think you will agree that this too is not realistic.
I therefore cannot see why the Progressive Conservatives voted against our amendment in that connection.
I have a letter which came to my desk this morning from the Retail Merchants Association of Canada. I am very happy to have this letter because it would appear that these people are now awakening to the situation prevailing in Canada. The C.C.F. have long been saying that we have an unbridled monopoly growth in Canada. It has now become apparent to the Retail Merchants Association of Canada that they are the victims of this unbridled free enterprise or capitalist system.
I just want to say that I sympathize with them. We have in this country, under the Combines Investigations Act, means by which certain monopoly growths are investigated, but I believe that there are not sufficient teeth in that legislation to prevent the unbridled growth of free enterprise and monopoly in this country. I am sure that all that has resulted from the numerous investigations we have had is a great many minor prosecutions, and more and more monopoly growth throughout Canada.
It reminds me of an article I saw some years ago in Time magazine on the barbotte games which were purported to be running in Montreal. Apparently down there the authorities would fine the barbotte gamblers in one place, and they would take their gambling to another part of the city and the game would go on. So it is with these people today. There is always some way in which they can squeeze out from under the act and continue their monopolistic functions in this country.
