Now what is the proper place for the retailers in Canada? We have two financial tycoons in this country grabbing more and more of the retail business of Canada. One of them is prominent in the bakery trade; another is a prominent distiller in this country. Here we have three or four monopolistic chain stores with their interlocking directorates which are going to control the biggest portion of the Canadian retail trade. Nothing is going to stop it as long as we have a government opposite which does not take any sufficient action to prevent this sort of thing.
I believe that the small retail people have their backs to the wall. We have this growth of chain stores and monopoly retailers who have many things to their advantage. This of course is causing the liquidation of the small retailer. The idea is always put forward by the old party spokesmen that we do not and should not have planning in this country, but I say that there is planning now. There is planning, a great deal of planning, by the big boys, the chain stores and their interlocking directorates. Therefore we are having the small retailer pushed to the wall and this government sits idly back just making punitive efforts to prevent it. A handful of large retailers will soon control the bulk of the retail trade of Canada. These companies have practically unlimited financial resources and the small retailers are handicapped by the lack of adequate credit for modernization.
I would like to put a word in for the prairie merchants because there is nothing that concerns me more than the situation which is facing many of our small retail merchants in the prairies. They have over the years been giving their farmers and their other patrons credit by means of which they can carry on until the grain is sold from the farms. These small retailers are the backbone of our western communities and they often give credit, but this government has not seen fit to give credit to the farmers through cash advances to enable the farmer to get some money until he can sell his grain and meet his obligations.
The C.C.F. stands alone on the policy of national planning. Other parties believe in and support unbridled free enterprise, but I believe that the time is coming when we have people like the Retail Merchants Association of Canada realizing that only through national planning can we have a system by which the small enterpriser can be protected. I therefore hope that this government will take into consideration some of the things I have mentioned this afternoon and that it will not allow our small enterprisers-among them our retail merchants associations-to be driven to the wall simply through the growth of monopoly which combines its interlocking

The Budget-Mr. MacLean directorates. I think this is a grave need; there is nothing in the budget and nothing in federal legislation to prevent this and it is a question which has to be answered by this government.
The C.C.F. believe in the protection of the small businessman; they believe in planning. We believe in three types of public ownership, as well as in private ownership. We believe in national ownership of those things which lend themselves to national ownership and which by their national importance and nature can properly be handled by national government. Equally so, we believe in provincial planning and provincial ownership of those things such as power and transportation of certain kinds, which lend themselves to provincial public ownership. Furthermore, we believe in public ownership through cooperation. One of the finest ways of living is for people to join themselves together in co-operative organization, to give themselves service at cost. I am happy to say that our province is going forward by leaps and bounds through co-operative ownership of various types of retail sales and enterprises.
Of course, last and tremendously important is our belief in private ownership; but as long as we have the unbridled free enterprise system, with the government taking no part in the prevention of the growth of monopoly and where we have, as I say, these interlocking directorates, they become so powerful that they finally push the small enterpriser to the wall. That is what is taking place.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say this. Now that we are coming to another election I hope that more and more people will see that national planning is necessary in order to give them protection and security in their homes and businesses.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in this debate I would like first to consider what is the proper thing that one might expect to find in a budget. I think I am correct in assuming that a parliamentary budget is, or should be, a collection of the proposals which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) puts before parliament for adjusting the revenue of the country to meet the expenditures. It should be, I think, nothing more and nothing less, traditionally and historically, than what it is, and these proposals are put forward in the form of resolutions to be considered by the committee of ways and means. As everybody knows, originally the committee of ways and means was a committee set up for the purpose of considering ways and means of providing supply to be granted to Her Majesty. This being the case, the proposals for


the expenditure of extra funds strictly speaking, in my opinion, are not proposals which properly should find their way into the budget.
When preparing a few notes for this brief speech, I looked over in a cursory manner the budget speeches of the last 50 years and I found that up until very recently there was nothing in the budget speeches except those things which properly belonged there, such as proposed changes in various taxes, tariffs and so on, together of course with a review of the economy of the country for the year before. This year's budget includes some proposals for extra expenditures. So far as the members of the house are concerned, those are very welcome proposals but they are proposals which do not come under the jurisdiction of the committee of ways and means and therefore should not properly be part of the budget. They are proposals that, more properly, might have been made in the speech from the throne. As the situation stands, these proposals having to do with increases in pensions of various kinds, cannot be brought into effect by the committee of ways and means but will have to be brought into effect by separate pieces of legislation. It is not my intention, therefore, Mr. Speaker, to dwell at any length on such proposals made by the Minister of Finance in the course of his budget speech. I suspect that possibly one of the reasons for putting them there was to clothe what might be the program of the party to which the minister belongs with the prestige of being part of the budget proposal which, in fact, they are not.
Many of these proposals will not be effective until a new parliament is elected. They can only be brought into effect by the next parliament or by legislation passed by this parliament before it prorogues. This legislation is not dealt with by the committee of ways and means. It is possible that the Minister of Finance might have assumed that since these proposals will not become effective until later in the year the general public might be persuaded to give some hostages to fortune with regard to them, and might confuse in their minds the return of this government with the coming into effect of these resolutions.
I am not suggesting from a parliamentary rules point of view that it is out of order for the minister to discuss such things in his budget speech, because we are given very wide latitude in this debate, but I am suggesting that it is not very good practice from the point of view of presenting a budget. I do not intend to give very much attention to the proposals contained in the minister's speech concerning the additional expenditure

of money except to say that the increases in old age pensions, family allowances, veterans pensions and so forth, although very small, are a step in the right direction. Nevertheless, it should not be forgotten that even with these increases the purchasing power of the pension and family allowance received will not be anything like as great as it was when these various measures came into effect. This is, of course, due to the inflationary trend in which we are living. So far as veterans are concerned they are still not in a satisfactory position, even when these increases come into effect, as compared to other segments of the country so far as income is concerned.
Having said that, I want to turn to some subjects which could properly, I think, be placed in a budget. One has to do with tariffs and in that connection I refer to one aspect of tariffs, a proposal which I hope will be put forth in the near future for some adjustment of the tariff between Canada and the United States on potatoes. This adjustment should be made at the earliest possible moment. I realize that negotiations may not be complete and the government may not be in a position to introduce an amendment to the tariff on United States potatoes coming into Canada in the committee of ways and means. If that is the case, I sincerely hope that the government will find some means whereby authority may be given to the governor in council to impose a tariff as soon as negotiations are completed. If that cannot be done and there is no protection given our potato growers until the next session of parliament, it will be too late to effect any benefits for the next crop year.
As hon. members know, United States potatoes come into Canada duty free for all but six weeks of each year, while Canadian potatoes going into the United States pay a tariff of 37.5 cents per hundredweight for a certain quota and then a greater tariff over that quota. Under this situation we have the protection of a tariff so far as the United States is concerned and free trade so far as Canada is concerned. This situation is intolerable because when there is overproduction of potatoes in the United States and the price falls they just push their surplus on to the Canadian market depressing the price on the Canadian market below the cost of production.
The threat of the import of United States potatoes under those conditions has a very destructive effect upon our market, even if there are no actual imports, and at the present time there are very considerable imports of United States potatoes into Canada. I hold in my hand the daily report on the potato market for the days of last week, and I should like
The Budget-Mr. MacLean to quote some of the figures. As far as the Montreal market is concerned the arrival of potatoes there is expressed in terms of carloads. The figures for last Monday, which include the arrivals for the previous Friday, were: from Prince Edward Island, 21 cars; from New Brunswick, 27 cars; from Maine, 2; and from California, 3. The next day on the Montreal market we have again, from Prince Edward Island, 9; from New Brunswick, 20; from Florida, 1 only; from Maine, 9. The next day we have, from Prince Edward Island, 7; from New Brunswick, 26; from California, 1; from Maine, 3. The next day we have, from Prince Edward Island, 11; from New Brunswick, 15; from Maine, 1. On Friday of last week we find in parenthesis "C.N. only". I am not sure of the significance of that. It shows from Prince Edward Island, 5; from New Brunswick, 3; from Maine, 7; and from Florida, 1.
I think that makes a total of about 30 carloads of United States potatoes arriving on the Montreal market in the space of one week and that tends, naturally, to have a very depressing effect on the market. As a matter of fact, it puts the Canadian producer at a disadvantage compared with the United States producer because of the rate of exchange. Although the potatoes may be sold for the same amount of money, the United States grower gets slightly more for them than the Canadian grower, even if their costs are equal, owing to the rate of exchange. Then as far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, the freight charges to the Montreal market are no doubt greater than they would be from Maine. That puts the Prince Edward Island grower in an unfavourable position. As far as prices are concerned, the Maine potatoes are underselling Prince Edward Island potatoes by a matter of 5 cents to 10 cents, or something of that sort, for a 50-pound bag.
I just wish, as forcibly as I possibly can, to point out to the government the vital importance of correcting this situation as far as the Canadian producer is concerned and as far as the general consuming public of Canada are concerned because if, for lack of protection, the Canadian potato producer is forced out of business, then the Canadian consumer will have to pay through the nose for United States potatoes at a later time because the supplies required will not be produced in Canada much longer under present conditions.
Having said that, I wish to turn now for a little while to the question of federal-provincial finances and the tax-sharing agreements between the provinces on the one hand and the federal government on the other as they affect the province from which I come, namely Prince Edward Island. I do

The Budget-Mr. MacLean not raise this subject in any partisan way or for any partisan purposes, but merely to point out to the government the desperate situation-and I do not think that is too strong a word-that my province finds itself in as far as provincial finances are concerned.
Since 1949 the provincial debt of Prince Edward Island has gone up from $15.4 million to $22.5 million at the present time. The other day the provincial treasurer, when bringing down his budget, budgeted for a deficit of $1.8 million, I think it was. It is true that the province of Prince Edward Island receives a considerable percentage of its budgetary income from the federal government in the form of subsidies and taxes gathered for it under the tax-rental agreements; but, unfortunately, fixed charges on the provincial government for services which it cannot avoid are so high that the province is constantly going deeper and deeper into debt. This naturally means an increased cost for servicing that debt. At the present time the cost of servicing the debt is almost equal to the forecast deficit for the year ahead.
Under the present tax-rental agreements- and I have studied them fairly carefully- I find that an adjustment of the payments made over the last five years must be made on the basis of the last census of 1956. During the last five years the dominion bureau of statistics has badly over-estimated the population of the province, with the result, as far as I can calculate it, that the payments to the province of Prince Edward Island under the last tax-rental agreement are considerably greater than they should have been. These agreements require that in such a case adjustment must be made between the last day of February and the last day of April this year. I do not know what the actual figures are, but on making a rough calculation on the population of Prince Edward Island that was made public from the 1956 census I came to the conclusion that the overpayment has probably been of the order of $1 million.
If that is so, this overpayment, when adjusted, would wipe out entirely the quarterly payment which would normally fall due at about this time under the tax-rental agreement. I believe that must be so, although the Minister of Finance has not yet given the details. I would not be surprised if the whole quarterly payment would not be enough to meet the requirements of the readjustment. It may be, although I do not know, that the government of Prince Edward Island will still owe the federal government some amount to compensate for the adjustment in the payments.


This is a very sorry and difficult state of affairs for my province because this will mean that it is not only poor but it is over $1 million poorer than it thought it was. In this case the province will be in debt by the end of next year not by $23.9 million but by something over $25 million which is a very heavy debt considering the small population of the province.
It may appear strange to some that I am devoting so much time to this question and it may be considered that it is not even a suitable question to be discussed on the budget because, as some may say, this is a matter to be worked out by the provincial government on the one hand and the federal government on the other. According to newspaper reports of proceedings in the legislature in Charlottetown, the premier has indicated that he considers this is a responsibility of the members of the federal parliament who come from that province. I am glad to assume at least a little of the responsibility in bringing to the attention of the federal government the necessity for more favourable terms as far as provincial-federal tax agreements are concerned.
The other day I saw a leading editorial in the Globe and Mail the heading of which was, "Mr. Garson, Meet Mr. MacDonald", and it started out by referring to a statement made by the Minister of Justice in the house to the effect that he thought the difficulties under which some provinces laboured were caused, to paraphrase the phrase he used as I recall it, by an occupational disease of Conservative governments. When I saw this heading, "Mr. Garson, Meet Mr. MacDonald", I could not think what Mr. MacDonald was meant. First I thought of Sir John A. Macdonald and another possibility was the late Angus L. Macdonald but I found that the gentleman referred to was the Hon. Earl MacDonald, the provincial treasurer of Prince Edward Island, who expressed views entirely different from those expressed by the Minister of Justice. The explanation given by the Minister of Justice for the difficulties encountered by some provinces cannot possibly apply to Prince Edward Island because there has been in power in that province for over 20 years a government which no doubt would be his choice if he were a resident of that province.
I am not suggesting for one moment that the provincial government there is entirely free of blame as far as the financial situation of the province is concerned; I think it would be unfair to do so. On the other hand I think it would be even more unfair to suggest that they are mostly to blame because I think most of the responsibility for this situation rests with the federal government in that the tax rental agreements are calculated on a formula

which is unfair to those parts of Canada which are not experiencing any degree of prosperity at the present time.
The adjustments which I feel will have to be made in the payments at the present time are due to the fact that the province of Prince Edward Island has not been able to retain the natural increase in its population because of the unsatisfactory economic conditions existing there. If the economic conditions were improved the tax rental agreements as they exist would come nearer to being satisfactory because if the natural increase in the population of my province could be retained there the per capita debt would be much lower and that increased population could be serviced at a cost the increase of which would be much less than the potential increase in revenue resulting from that situation.
If steps were taken by this government to give equality of opportunity to all Canadians regardless of whether they live in the mari-times, Ontario, Saskatchewan or elsewhere, the tax rental agreements might then function as they were intended to or more nearly so, but the maritimes have been experiencing difficult times economically and this adds to their difficulties as far as financing provincial governments is concerned.
My province is in the unhappy situation where the provincial government states it is unable financially to accept the hospital insurance proposals of the federal government. That creates the situation where the poor are made poorer so to speak, because although the provincial government of Prince Edward Island cannot go into this scheme neither can they wave a magic wand and prevent people from having to go to hospital. The result is that as individuals the people of my province will be worse off than the rest of the people in this country because they will have to pay their hospital costs themselves and still contribute to the normal taxes which are paid into the federal government, none of which will be paid back for this hospital scheme in their case.
It seems absolutely imperative to me, that steps be taken at the earliest possible time to give equality of opportunity to all Canadians. As far as the maritimes are concerned steps must be taken to encourage industry there and to protect the agricultural industry so that the natural increase in population can be retained in those provinces.
As a direct assistance to the maritime provinces I would strongly recommend that the statutory subsidies to the various provinces be readjusted in the light of the decreased value of the Canadian dollar. I believe the subsidies are completely unrealistic not
The Budget-Mr. Holowach only because of the fact that the value of the dollar has decreased but also because the cost of government has increased tremendously since these subsidies were last adjusted. If that were done on a generous scale the maritime provinces would then be in a less unsatisfactory position as far as the tax rental agreements are concerned, but I believe there is room for adjustment in both fields.
I think it is vitally important as far as tax rental agreements are concerned that a more accurate system be devised for estimating population, especially of the smaller provinces, so that they do not find themselves in the position where they have overpaid in the past and then have to make up for it when the readjustment is made. After all, in my province the budgets have been made for the last five years on the basis of the estimated payments made over these years. The readjustment of over $1 million places the province in a most unsatisfactory situation at the present time.
I should point out that I reached that figure as the result of my own calculation. I am not absolutely sure that my calculations are accurate, but I think they are, and if that is the case I do feel that the Minister of Finance should try to find some emergency means for softening the blow, at least so far as the provincial government is concerned, or, better still if it is possible, work out some formula whereby this figure, whatever it is, will not have to be deducted from the aggregate payment made to that province during the life of the 1952 tax rental agreement, because we are the province which of all provinces can least afford it.

Mr. Speaker, among the important debates we have had so far this session this present discussion takes a leading place. The 1957 budget proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on March 14 is the largest in Canada's peace-time history. It calls for federal expenditure amounting to $5,170 million for the fiscal year 1957-58. Last year the surplus was $300 million, and this year a further large surplus is proposed, a surplus far in excess of anticipated expenditure, which means an ever-rising tide of federal taxation.
There are several very serious implications in these figures, and I welcome the opportunity of joining my colleagues in the Social Credit group in a further presentation of our convictions and of some indisputable facts. I do so because we were sent here by our citizens to fight for a positive program for all of Canada, and I believe, sir, that not even by the widest stretch of imagination

The Budget-Mr. Holowach can we say that such a program is before us now. The budget under discussion is in fact a statement of the social and fiscal policies of the present Liberal administration.
For several days now we have heard arguments for and against these proposals. It is natural in a debate of this kind that members who support the government should consider it their main function to congratulate the Minister of Finance. It is their privilege and their right to do this. But we cannot take their remarks too seriously when we consider the number of impressive facts and harsh realities which have been swept under the carpet.
We have examined the budget carefully, and I cannot help but feel, such is the impression it leaves, that it meets the requirements of only those who are financially secure-the fortunate and privileged few in this country. But we are not here to legislate only on behalf of one particular group. As for myself, I was sent here to represent all the people, and to act on their behalf, particularly that element which believes that government policies are denying it a fair share of well-being and the rights it should possess. Analysed in the light of the economic situation which affects my constituents-and I think this applies generally in Canada-in the light of the situation which faces the labouring man, the white collar worker, the small businessman, the old age pensioner, the blind, the veteran, all those who depend for their livelihood on fixed incomes, and the womenfolk of Canada who have the heavy responsibility of building happy homes in this country, 1 say that these proposals are nothing more than a cynical act of unreality.
The people are aware of their problems. Why is this government not aware of them? It has always been my conviction that the purpose of government is to make life easier for the people. It has always been my belief that governments should help in solving the economic and social problems which need solution. There is no evidence in this budget before us to indicate that this government is so inclined.
It is time to take stock of our national affairs. Instead of tackling the problem by introducing safe and sane policies, it seems to me that the government's attitude is one of unreality and wishful thinking. I recognize that shortage of time will make it impossible to cover many of the issues to which I would like to refer, but I wish today to consider two basic issues arising from this budget. One is economic, the other is moral. With respect to the first, I draw attention to the ever-rising cost of living, the menace

of price inflation, the lessening of purchasing power of the dollar, tight money, the credit squeeze, usurious interest rates, the high operating costs of business, the increasing burden of excessive taxation, the unretarded growth of government and its monopolies, the centralization of more and more taxation power in Ottawa and the hypothecation of future income to pay for instalment living.
These are the problems that are left unanswered and unchecked by the latest budget. It is with this in mind as background that we are obliged to join with all the rest of those who have condemned the budget. Let us look at some of the items I have mentioned a little closer. With respect to the increasing cost of living and price inflation, we read of this each day in our newspapers. Here is a clipping from the Edmonton Journal of December 4, 1956, with the heading: "Cost of Living Index Climbs to New Record." A few weeks later, in an edition dated January 4, 1957, of the same newspaper we find this heading: "Living Cost Index is Still Climbing." And a few weeks later still: "Living Index Hits New High".
An article in the Edmonton Journal of March 5, 1957, reads as follows:
Ottawa (CP)-Living costs rose again in January pushing the consumer price index to a record 120.5, an increase of one-fifth of a point from 120.3 in December.
Main propelling forces for the rise which followed a slight decline in December, were higher prices for gasoline, drugs, personal care items and alcoholic beverages, the bureau of statistics reported today. The index is based on 1949 prices equalling 100.
A substantial advance in hospital room rates also contributed to an increase in the other commodities and services sub-index from 123.1 to 123.8.
The over-all index figure of 120.5 at February 1 represents a gain of 4.1 points over the same date in 1956.
The food sub-index in January rose to 117.2 from 117.1. Numerous slight increases for most foods were nearly offset by somewhat larger price decreases for coffee, eggs, lettuce and tomatoes. The only food item to register a significant price increase was sugar.
The shelter sub-index moved up from 133.6 in December to 133.8 in January as a result of small increases in both the rent and home ownership components.
The only sub-index to decline was clothing which dropped from 107.6 in December to 107.4 in January. Sale prices for women's winter coats and overshoes and boys' parkas outweighed a further increase in the price of men's suits.
Price increases for fuel oil and a number of items of furniture, textiles and utensils pushed the household operation sub-index to 119.1 from 119.0.
What do all these figures indicate? They simply mean, Mr. Speaker, that the workingman's hard earned dollar is buying less and less for him and his family. They mean that higher prices for food, clothing and fuel are hurting the poor much more than the well to

do. Where is all this going to lead us? I predict that if these increases continue to mount we will soon all have to hold out our palms to Ottawa. Is there an answer to this problem in the budget? There is no evidence that there is.
We cannot go along with the government's claim that the situation is due to too much money chasing too few goods. Will someone name any consumable goods that are in short supply in our country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I never said that.

Quite the contrary, the only thing that we have in short supply is a sane and sensible economic policy at the administrative level. There are plenty of goods, as evidenced by our gross national product, goods of every variety and kind. We have the paradox of consumers facing ever-rising prices while producers and farmers are facing falling incomes. In what way is the budget resolving this paradox? The fact is that government taxation and monetary policies have contributed to it more than anything else. Excessive fatty layers of invisible taxes incorporated into the prices of goods have raised the prices of these goods to an all-time high.
In addition to the heavy taxation policy of the government, taxation which is far in excess of required revenues, the government authorities have instituted a tight money policy which has resulted in Bank of Canada interest rate hoists seven times during the last year and a half. It is difficult for any Canadian to understand on what authority the minister thinks this is desirable. For one thing, it has already resulted in higher everything, including an increase of some $22 million in the interest charges on the public debt. In 1956 the interest on the public debt was $492,600,000 and it is estimated that in 1957 it will cost $522,200,000. For another thing, it has resulted in higher interest rates on loans for school and hospital construction, and the same applies to municipal borrowings. Our newspapers are full of such items.
I should like to say a little more about this business of inflation. Speaking in Toronto on January 28, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) stated that Canadians ought to save more and spend less. I refer to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of January 29 headed, "Must Save More and Spend Less." The article reads in part as follows:
Finance Minister Harris says Canadians should save more and spend less to maintain the present economy and prevent inflation.
On March 14 the minister again implied that this was the cure for inflation. It would be commendable if the government for which he speaks would practice exactly what he
The Budget-Mr. Holowach preaches but instead it advocates tight money for the little man on the street back home and plenty of flush money for the ever-growing bureaucracy at Ottawa. It just does not make sense. Furthermore, it is a little hard for the public to feel happy when the government extracts over $5 billion of their purchasing power and then piously whispers to them, "Spend less, save more."
There is no issue more paramount so far as our people are concerned at this time than the incredible burden of direct and invisible taxes they must carry. In the first place, taxes are at the bankruptcy point. They are weakening the people's capacity to save and manage their own affairs. In spite of this the government persists in demanding heavy taxation even though it collected a budgetary surplus of $300 million in 1956-57 and is budgeting for a surplus of $152 million in 1957-58.
I say to the minister in all earnestness that a continuation of the present rate of taxation is more dangerous to the preservation of our way of life than any outside threat. If this sounds a little too harsh, let me say to the minister that more and more centralization of taxation powers in Ottawa will place us on the same road as that which has taken many nations into serious trouble. All we have to do is to look at the pages of history to justify the truth of that statement.
But there is another matter. There is something wrong about a situation which is not a reflection of the people concerned. The harried taxpaying public are widely aroused that their pleas for reasonable reductions have been ignored. In making a plea for a fairer tax structure I again urge the minister to reconsider the matter. I again urge that there should be a complete overhaul of our entire taxation structure and a substantial reduction in those taxes that are a detriment, first, to saving, second, to consumption and, third, to production and investment.
One of the greatest needs of all is tax exemption on essential foodstuffs, clothing and materials of shelter. These are the things which the Canadian people want, but the government answers by doing away with the 10 per cent sales tax on chewing gum, candy, soft drinks, septic tanks and window screens. The vast surpluses which the government is piling up indicate that the government seems to believe that lowering taxes will result in the public undertaking unessential spending. What sort of conceit is this? This attitude ignores the fact that the people of Canada are honest and have greater wisdom than the wisdom of their government. Tax reductions will be used to extract people from debt and will provide

The Budget-Mr. Holowach future security for many of them. They will create capital for new business ventures and provide jobs. They will enable people to make sound investments instead of looking on helplessly while foreign capital takes over what should have been their own investments.
But economic considerations are not the only issue before us. There is a moral issue. We founded our country upon the basic principle that governments will be enlightened and apply high, ethical standards in high office. In this connection it is right that we should evaluate the plight of our senior citizens, the blind and the veterans. I know that the old age pensioners will be pleased to receive the extra $6 proposed in the budget, but the ratio of inflation to the cost of living makes that a niggardly amount. It is only a tiny patch on what has always been a threadbare pension. Surely this administration knows that $46 does not even provide enough money for a proper subsistence diet. The total cost of this boost in payments to old age pensioners 70 and over will be some $45 million, the price of one nuclear-powered submarine or half a dozen heavy jet bombers.
Why has the government waited so long, until the eve of an election, to come forward with a helping hand? That is a question which I should like to have someone answer. The advancing of $6 and the offering of it on the eve of an election show that the administration gives not on the basis of merit or need, but simply on the basis of political expediency. Good government ought not to be playing with the welfare of the old age pensioners and the veterans.
The Ottawa Journal of March 15, 1957 contains an editorial in which I think the writer strikes the nail right on the head. It is entitled "The True Nature of the Budget". I should like to read a brief quotation from it:
The true measure of responsible social security is in a balance between what is socially desirable and economically feasible.
The measure to social security applied by Mr. Harris' budget is what may be politically profitable -profitable for the government in an election.
Relief of need is of humanitarian importance. On that ground no one can or should oppose an increase of pensions for the aged, for war veterans, or for the blind.
But the aged, the war veterans and the blind have been in dire need of help these past three years; have had to struggle for existence under a dollar worth less than two-thirds of its value only a few years ago.
Why did the government, taxing and spending and still reaping large surpluses, wait until now to offer relief?

speechtext: Because it is obvious. My hon. friend is reading from an editorial, I believe; and thereby I take it that he is sponsoring the accuracy of that editorial.
I am sponsoring-

speechtext: The accuracy of the editorial.
-the idea and the ideal for which this editorial stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There were not large surpluses in the last two years, as the editorial says. There were deficits in the last two years.

There were surpluses last year, and the government is planning for substantial surpluses for the coming year. The article further states:
All of us know the answer. The government could have done last year or the year before what it did on Thursday-the money was in its till. But there was no election last year or the year before and there is one this year.
That is what is happening to social security in this country:	A desirable thing, a humanitarian
problem, something which should be weighed in the scales of social justice and economic possibility, is being degraded into a political weapon.
Governments in days past had to raise election funds. There is no need for that now. The present government gets its campaign funds by dipping into the public treasury, timing social security measures to general elections-the needy only incidental beneficiaries.
And then the Journal further comments:
The Journal would like to think, dares even to hope, that pensioners and others thrown at the eleventh hour of the election what they should have been given long ago will resent this attempt to buy their votes-scorn this insult to their intelligence.
I should like to tell the minister that we were pleased that he has given some attention to the needy and to the problems of the veterans; they certainly deserve it. May I tell him this. In any further consideration of their needs let us remember that it is not enough to dislike poverty amongst them and to denounce it. The government must put some conscientious effort into improving their lot in the same way that these people put conscientious effort into winning the war.
There are several other matters upon which I should like to touch briefly. The first is the question of discriminatory freight rates about which I have spoken on previous occasions in this house. We were glad to hear that some assistance to the maritimes on the matter of freight rates is now being considered, but I must confess that I was disappointed to learn that such assistance and review are not being given to the western provinces. On previous occasions I have pointed out the discriminatory freight rates against my own province which are impeding our industrial growth. The fact is that no other place in Canada has such exorbitant freight rates and this state of affairs has been going on for a long time. The people of Alberta demand that something be done to halt the unfairness of our whole freight rate structure. With that in mind, I was amazed

when the other day on the orders of the day this question was asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), as reported at page 2640 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Transport. Now that the government has announced that a comprehensive examination of the entire transportation system of the Atlantic provinces will be made in order to determine what can be done to contribute to their welfare, will a similar comprehensive examination of the system on the prairies be carried out in order to assist the economic welfare of that region and to remove the discriminatory freight rates?
Here is the answer given by the Minister of Transport:
Mr. Speaker, I would repudiate the suggestion that there is any possible comparison outside of the mind of the hon. gentleman between the two areas which have just been mentioned. I cannot think at the moment of any reason why the government should consider making an inquiry into transportation conditions in the west.
That is an amazing statement. Everyone knows that one of the most vicious inequities in our country is the freight rates which Canadians of western Canada are paying at this time. This is what the Liberal government has condoned and supported:
On March 30, 1948: the transport board authorized a general freight rate increase of 21 per cent.
October 12, 1948: the federal cabinet disposed of the appeal against the 21 per cent increase by refusing to revoke the increase.
May 11, 1950: the transport board authorized a further general increase in freight rates of 20 per cent.
June 24, 1950: the provinces-all but Ontario and Quebec-presented an appeal to the federal cabinet against the 20 per cent increase.
November 29, 1950: the federal cabinet dismissed the appeal of the provinces.
January 25. 1952: the transport board authorized a further general freight increase of 17 per cent.
December 20, 1952: the transport board authorized a further general freight rate increase of 9 per cent.
March 6, 1953: the transport board authorized a further general freight rate increase of 7 per cent.
May 1, 1953: the provinces-all except Ontario and Quebec-appeared before the federal cabinet upon an appeal against the 7 per cent increase.
Last year the federal government authorized a further 11 per cent increase. We are paying freight both ways. We are paying on everything coming in and on everything going out; and the Liberal government which has supported all these increases over a short period of time pyramiding freight rates to an all-time high gouging western producers and consumers tells us there is no inequity in the situation. How in the world does this Liberal government expect to elect any Liberal members in the province of Alberta?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: They don't.

Members of the Liberal government in this house, no matter how well meaning they are, must support and condone these discriminatory policies against the western prairie provinces.
The Budget-Mr. Holowach
What about the small businessman, the mainstay of the free enterprise system and effective competition? In my own community I know of several businessmen who have gone out of business because of the credit squeeze. We in the Social Credit group will continue to voice our determination to end the economic squeeze. The government should extend some tax relief to the small businessman and give priority to him in the matter of the small loans that he needs to stay in business.
The hardest hit field is residential construction. With respect to this my own community of Edmonton is experiencing one of the worst homebuilding snags in its history. Since it is one of the fastest growing cities in Canada homes are urgently needed but statistics show that discriminatory federal policies and high finance charges have resulted in fewer houses being started in Edmonton than the average number in any other place in Canada.
It is all very well for the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) to talk about the number of homes that were built in 1955-56, but the fact remains that this government is dragging its feet and not enabling Canadians to secure mortgage money on attractive terms so that they can acquire homes. In what way does this budget propose to solve this serious problem. I say to you that if this budget is the Liberal government's answer to some of the serious problems I have mentioned then the people of Canada must resign themselves to the solemn conviction that this government will not act differently. It is confused and does not know what to do or else it has been in power for so long that it now feels it is boss and can defy the will of its own people.
The lesson to be learned is that there is indeed the need for a political alternative. We earnestly hope that the people of Canada will seize the only practical and sensible alternative, and that alternative is the principle and the platform of the Social Credit party. We have demonstrated what a businesslike government can accomplish in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. No other provinces in Canada enjoy such a healthy economic climate. With such an alternative, with a country that is so richly endowed with a vigorous and talented people, endowed with vast resources; with the vision and the will to do it, Canada can not only remain the country of the free but the people of this country can be the envy of the entire world.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question, if he does not mind, before he takes his seat. It is only in the interests of accuracy and not a matter of opinion. I thought he said I had removed the sales tax on candy and chewing gum. If

The Budget-Mr. W. M. Howe that is so, I ask him does he not realize that it was the special excise tax on candy?
I appreciate the correction. I meant the excise tax.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this budget debate feeling that it is one of the most important annual debates to take place in this House of Commons. Since this is the fifth budget of this 22nd parliament of Canada, no doubt it has special significance for all parts of Canada because of the fact this is an election year. The budget is doubly important in that it not only sums up and gives a resume of the year's financial events but it also makes a forecast as to the financial events of the coming year. The bringing down of the budget is an event that is looked forward to by people from all walks of life whether they represent big business or little business; whether they be professional people or ordinary workers, farmers or industrialists, because changes or proposed changes in the budget can affect the income, prosperity and happiness of every individual in Canada.
As I indicated previously, the budget has been looked forward to with greater anticipation this election year than in any other year because individuals and organizations, wage earners and small industrialists, pensioners and farmers are all looking forward to long-awaited changes. The pensioner is looking forward to changes in the pension setup, whether it be old age, veterans, blind or disabled pensions. The farmer is looking forward to some revision in the price support legislation in order to balance the selling price of his products with his cost of operation. The small businessman, and the farmer as well, are looking forward to an easing of credit restrictions which are just about driving them out of business.
I feel that this year also the members on the government benches were looking forward to the budget in the hope that the tremendous surplus indicated in the white paper of a few years ago would be used to reestablish their positions all across Canada which have been so shaken and so disrupted by the defence production bill of 1955 and the pipe-line debate of 1956. They were hoping that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) would pull a few rabbits out of his budgetary hat to relieve the pressure and ensure their return. But what did they get? They did not get a rabbit to allay all their fears and worries but a rarebit-a bits and pieces budget that tries to do all things for too many people. No doubt every member in the house welcomes the fact that at long last

the government is beginning to appreciate and have consideration for the old age pensioners, as well as every other type of pensioner who has been caught in the terrific squeeze created by the mounting prices of the necessities of life. However, I cannot see how an additional $6 a month or approximately 20 cents a day is going to do very much for those on old age security.
The other day I had a letter from a constituent of mine who is 83 years of age and who has been living alone. He had been paying $36 per month board and his landlady wished to raise it to $40. Now that he has an increase in pension he will no doubt have to pay the $40. He will have, therefore, the magnificent sum of $6 per month additional. If he saves all his money for two months, he may have enough to buy a pair of shoes and a shirt. It will take another two months of saving to buy a pair of trousers. If he wants to buy a suit of even the cheapest quality he will have to save all his money for at least six months. When we get down to the facts and figures this increase is very unrealistic and will do little to ease the burden of those who are in the sunset of life.
There is no doubt that the reduction in the price of tea and coffee will assist some of those who have the regular coffee and tea breaks, but the reduction in the price of chocolate bars, candy and pop will be of no great advantage to the old gentleman of whom I spoke because he will not have any money to spend on them anyway.
It is interesting to note that bit by bit the government is listening to the requests of the opposition members with respect to the exemption from sales tax on articles and goods purchased by municipalities and associated boards, because a year or so ago certain road-building equipment was exempted, and now we find this year school desks and chairs, structural steel for bridges and precast concrete shapes have been exempted from sales tax. I still cannot understand why this government could not have gone the whole way and assisted the already over-burdened municipal taxpayer by abolishing this iniquitous form of double taxation of sales tax on municipal purchases.
In speaking of the people who were particularly looking forward to the bringing down of the budget this year, I mentioned the farmers of Canada. In the four years that I have been a member of this house there is one thing that I just cannot seem to understand, namely, the indifference of this government to the problems concerning the farmers from coast to coast. One wonders whether it is the wish of this government that more

and more farmers should be driven off the land. This action and this attitude are rather hard to understand. In a recent speech by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) he advised young farmers to stay on the land. I feel the Minister of Agriculture is right; that farming is a very healthy and satisfactory way of life, but of what value is it to be healthy if one cannot make a living, if one cannot earn enough money to hold up one's head in the community? He must be a part-time farmer in order to get enough cash to pay his interest and taxes, with the result that his farming operation fails. That is what is happening. Many of our young people are leaving the farms. To me this situation is becoming critical.
Our year book for 1956, brought up to date to 1954, quotes a few figures. The first one must have been inspired by the Minister of Agriculture, because it is in his usual way to gloss over a situation by quoting a five, six, seven or eight-year average. In the first paragraph on agriculture it is mentioned that in the last few years, from 1946 to 1953, farmers realized a net income of $1,611,600,000 from farming operations. This was for a seven-year period.
Farming represents the greatest basic industry in our country. When we realize that the value of farmlands and buildings, implements, machinery and livestock represent capital invested in some two-thirds of a million farms to a total of almost the $10 billion mark we understand how important this industry is. But it is also rather hard to understand just why so little has been done. Goodness knows, there has been enough said in this house about it. Year after year our farmers' organizations have appeared before the cabinet and caucuses of different parties with briefs, applications and suggestions for assistance that might be given. Practically every farm paper you pick up, or every editorial on farming, would indicate that something is wrong. We have experts saying that the small farmer is done, that he is inefficient. I resent that. I know that in my riding some of the most efficient farms are the small farms, where father, mother and children work together in trying to make a success of it. Men who have followed agriculture all their lives, good farmers, are selling their farms, as I learned last week, because they just cannot see any future in farming.
We find that in spite of their restricted numbers farmers are producing more and more each year, and if this government had a more realistic trade policy, if they had made greater efforts to retain the British markets for butter, cheese, beef and pork, the
The Budget-Mr. W. M. Howe farmers would be producing more than they are producing today, because they would realize that when it came time to market their produce there would be a foreign market for their surplus production. But in spite of all that I have said, in spite of all these representations, what do we find in the budget that will help the farmer, that will help him become more self-sufficient?
Reference is made to the fact that if conditions are normal this year it is expected that his income will equal that of 1951. Between 1952 and 1954 his income dropped practically $800 million, as indicated in the year book. Some reference was made to tariffs in the budget to assist the maritimes with the potato situation, and then to salve the feelings of the farmers' organizations that sent wires to practically every member of parliament representing an agricultural riding asking for an additional tariff on skim milk powder and cheese. The government's reply was that they are having continued talks with the Australian government on trade matters.
I might make this further comment. What do we find in the legislation this year? Practically no help is given to this industry which has reached such a sad state. There have been amendments to some acts, in fact, there is an amendment to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. The parliamentary assistant himself indicated that the reason it had to be amended was the accelerated demand for farm loans which in itself is an indication that farmers need assistance.
The other evening at the milk producers' banquet in the Chateau Laurier the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made a big fellow of himself by announcing a new floor price on skim milk powder. If he really wanted to do a job on dairy products why did he not go right across the board and raise the floor price on butter? This policy of the government of setting floor prices for butter two years ahead of time is definitely unrealistic. Fifty-eight cents was a fair price for butter probably last year, although I have a chart here which indicates that the average hourly income of a dairy farmer who sends his milk to creameries is 13 cents. However, this year, whether it is owing to the fact that we had too much rain, or to the fact that the farmers have not been able to afford to buy the necessary fertilizers, the grain and hay crops in eastern Canada did not contain proper nutritional values so that the farmer to maintain his cream production had to buy western feed grain and concentrates at $90 a ton, which many of them were unable to do, and so butter production has been dropping.

Before the house rose at six o'clock I had referred to the request made by the federation of agriculture that amendments be made to the farm products marketing act so that farmers might carry on their own self-help programs through producer marketing boards. Although this legislation has been promised, it has not yet appeared on the order paper. This indifference, this procrastination, this unrealistic approach to agricultural problems cannot continue or the time may come when we in Canada, despite our millions of acres of rich, arable land bequeathed to us, will become dependent on other countries of the world for food.
As I indicated previously, the small businessman and the small industrialist were also looking forward to some assistance from the budget and hoping that the tight money policy might be relaxed so that they could obtain the necessary credit to expand and improve their businesses in competition with the great chain organizations and shopping centres which, by means of give-aways, special discounts and trading stamps, are squeezing the small operator out of business, the man who has always been the backbone of the community, who has given not only service to his customers but has paid a major share of municipal taxes, has taken his place on municipal councils and associated boards and has donated to every worthy cause. The budget offers very little, if any, assistance for him.
Then there is another group I should like to bring to the attention of the house, the average wage earners, the white collar man and the factory employee whose incomes are low and who should have had consideration. I should like to join with all other hon. members who have suggested that the statutory exemptions should have been raised from $1,000 to $1,500 for a single man and from $2,000 to $3,000 for a married man in order to help these people to meet the increased cost of living.
The 20-year old age security residence rule is going to affect many new Canadians who

have become good citizens and are contributing to our increased production and to government revenues. In my opinion it should be changed to ten years. In fact, I know of a case involving a former constituent of mine who died recently and who came to Canada in 1923. In 1939 he returned to the Isle of Man for a visit. Because of the war and transportation difficulties he was not able to return to Canada until 1949 and therefore was not able to get the old age pension. He died last year at the age of 73. However, his widow is still alive and is living in straitened circumstances simply because of the 20-year residence rule applying to old age pensioners.
All these people whom I have mentioned are ordinary folk, but apparently they have been forgotten by the members of the government who appear to hide in their ivory tower. Do not forget that these are the people who decide elections and will be deciding on who shall form the government of Canada after June of this year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the time of confederation until the year 1957, there have been something like 90 budgets presented to parliament and countless numbers of words have been uttered. It is not the purpose of the member for St. Lawrence-St. George to add to that great flow of words to any great extent. First of all, if the member for St. Lawrence-St. George has not participated in those debates of particular interest to our western farmers it is not because the people of my constituency are lacking in a genuine interest in the problems of those who come from western Canada. In addition, if I as the member for St. Lawrence-St. George have not participated in debates of particular concern to members from the Atlantic provinces, involving particularly the fishermen and the miners, it is not because the citizens of St. Lawrence-St. George or their representative are unmindful of the particular problems of that section of the country.
One does not need to be a great student of economic affairs to say that if the farmers of western Canada, the fishermen on both coasts and in the inland waters of Canada, the trappers, those engaged in lumbering, if all these primary producers do not apply their labour to the natural resources of Canada we shall not long have economic well-being. Those of us who live in the city of Montreal just as those who live in the great city of Toronto or the city of Winnipeg-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Fort William.
The Budget-Mr. Richardson

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -or Fort William-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or Peterborough.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -are particularly concerned and genuinely interested in those problems which are of immediate concern to miners, fishermen and all others throughout Canada whom we regard as primary producers.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And then you vote against them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It also does not take a very profound student of economics to realize that in this era we have now come into what might be described as the stream of production. We find that our younger people, those in their late teens and early twenties, are out of the immediate stream of production because they are preparing themselves for their professions or occupations so that they may earn a livelihood. Then you find people all over the country who are immersed completely in the stream of production. They are active people who are applying their efforts and talents to the natural resources of Canada. Essentially it is they who create the economic wealth of the country.
Then there are those who are in their middle or late sixties or the seventies and have stepped out of the stream of production and are more or less sitting on the banks. They are retired, as is their right, while those in the middle part of the stream, in the active part of the stream of production, are producing the economic wealth from which and only from which this or any other parliament can find the ways and means, the revenue with which to provide for the estimates and pay for the measures of supply upon which we vote. We have encouraged our young people, and rightly so, to get more and more education and to prepare themselves better for the active part of the stream of production. Because of medical science and research people are living longer and can enjoy a greater portion of their lives in complete or semi-retirement.
But my only point here is that those of us who are charged as trustees in this principal legislative forum of Canada must not lose sight of the fact that the only place where we can obtain the taxes, the ways and means by which we can grant the estimates of supply and discharge what we regard as our social obligations, is from those people engaged in the active part of the great stream of production of the country, whether they be manual workers, entrepreneurs or people in the professions. Therefore when we are asked by the government of this country at this time to adjust the old age pensions and other

The Budget-Mr. Richardson pensions of the people who are in that third part of the stream, almost on the banks, certainly anybody who is at all sensitive to human needs is glad that these pensions or retirement benefits can be adjusted. As for myself, I do not know whether it should be $6 or whether it should be $10.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the cost of living increase?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will give you my answer; just be patient for a moment. I put a figure before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) announced it the other night and my hon. friend who sat beside me saw the figure. That figure, so far as I can mathematically adjust it, would be approximately $8.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that the cost of living increase?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Approximately; that is right. That is my answer in any event and I give it for myself. Certainly I should like to see many older people get many dollars. There is no doubt about that, and there is no great difficulty about discussing it. However we must remember that it is only from those people who are actively engaged in the production of the economic wealth of the country that we can raise the taxes, the revenue, whereby the educational grants to help the younger people and whereby to help the older people who have served their day, -let us not argue about that matter at this time-and who deserve first our compassion and second, all that we can pull from the stream of production to help them. There is no difficulty in arriving at that conclusion.
While Montreal is not a great land of waving corn, while it does not have many mines under the streets, and while the fish that are there are certainly not ones that you would want to eat, we are interested in all the problems of those who are in the field of primary production and in the extent to which we can make our contribution in the field of transportation, whereby we unload the grain that comes from western Canada; and whereby we unload the coal that comes from the mines of Nova Scotia; whereby we take the newsprint or the pulp and send it on its way to all parts of the world; in the fields of trade and commerce, distribution, transportation, finance and insurance. To the extent that we can grow with the rest of Canada, we are glad; and also to the extent that Canada grows even faster than Montreal, I am sure that man for man most of the constituents which I have the honour to represent would be glad in every way.
I want to deal at this juncture with one point raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo


(Mr. Cameron) who has just retired from the chamber, and this shows one of the difficulties of dealing with matters of finance. I do not pose as an expert in the field of banking or finance but the hon. member who was the first speaker for his party on this budget debate at page 2471 of Hansard referred to the question of what he calls the inequities in the 20 per cent rebate on income derived from Canadian corporation dividends. He went on to say this, if I may quote him for just a minute; and I do not want, Mr. Speaker, to be unkind to him. He can take care of himself.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are unkind.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He said this:
I want to put on record at this point some figures with regard to this because I have had great difficulty in persuading those citizens oi Canada whom I have had the opportunity to address that the government is actually doing what it is doing.
I have no doubt the Minister of Finance will be very pleased to know that the average Canadian citizen whom I have encountered virtually refuses to believe me when I recite the facts of the 20 per cent dividend income rebate. I have been told repeatedly by audiences that I must be confused, I must be wrong, . . .
Mr. Speaker, if you will be patient with me, I would like to show wherein he is confused and wherein he is wrong. It is a simple escape from a simple fact. He took two hypothetical taxpayers and adjusted their tax payments, one whom he said derived his income from dividends, the other from salary. I wish to take those two same hypothetical taxpayers and to over-simplify the problem for my hon. friend.
Of these two taxpayers, called A and B, A has saved some money, either through hard manual work in the coal mines or the steel mills or out on the western prairies-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or stolen it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. My hon. friend may have friends who get their money in that way but I do not have them. If my hon. friend wants to ask another question I will sit down and take it. The first taxpayer, taxpayer A, has saved some money usually from hard manual work-I stress the word "usually"-perhaps by dint of some education, perhaps by leaving school earlier and having taken an I.C.S. course or by working as a newsboy or in the steel mills, has made it on the side, but not as my hon. friend has suggested, stolen it at all.
That is taxpayer A and he gets together, as have many people throughout this Canada, a little sum of money and he starts a business; he chooses a corporate form of organization, not a sole proprietorship, not a partnership

but a corporation. For the purpose of oversimplification, but nonetheless the truth, he forms a company with himself as sole shareholder and then, because he wants somebody to work with him, he employs taxpayer B, the other hypothetical taxpayer referred to in the speech of the hon. member for Nanaimo. He employs him and he employs him at the figure suggested by the hon. member, namely, $11,133. The figures which I shall use are round figures but the principle is exactly the same.
This taxpayer A now has formed a company; he is the only shareholder and he has one salaried employee, namely the other hypothetical taxpayer B. Now it follows that in order for there to be a dividend there must be a company. In order for there to be a dividend there must be a net profit and so that the record will be clear, and so my hon. friend will read it carefully in Hansard tomorrow, may I point out that A as shareholder of the company takes all the business risks and employs B, guaranteeing his salary of $11,133.
Now what happens? To make a dividend for A the company has to have a gross income of $25,050; B is paid his salary of $11,133, leaving $13,917 net taxable income on which a tax at the rate of 20 per cent is paid, that tax amounting to $2,783. That then leaves a profit in the hands of taxpayer A, the sole shareholder of the company who is employing B, and that is paid to him as a dividend of $11,133.
The net result then is that A takes his remuneration by way of dividend, in effect as a sole shareholder, and pays $2,783 in tax, while B, the paid employee, pays, as the hon. member said a few days ago, $1,877. On reflection and upon reading this tomorrow, my hon. friend will find that, unlike the illustration he gave the other day in which he suggested the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) should remit four cents to one of his hypothetical taxpayers, we now see that because he takes into account the fact that the company in order to have dividends must have profits, must have some work behind it, the taxpayer who takes the business risks will have paid something like $906 more in taxes than the other hypothetical taxpayer.
I do not make these remarks for the edification of my fellow friends here. I do not pose as any great expert in the field of economics, in the field of finance or even in the field of taxes. I simply believe it is only right that we who have been granted the right and the privilege of speaking for the 16 million people of Canada should hesitate every time before we speak in order that we may not tell to
The Budget-Mr. Richardson the people of Canada or to our colleagues in this house what is worse than a lie-this has no reference to my hon. friend and I apply it to myself as quickly as he would apply it to himself-and that, I suggest, is that we do not tell half truths.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what we are hearing now.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all, but if the hon. gentleman or one of his colleagues wants to speak after me I shall stand to be corrected. I might say that is one way in which these suggestions go out to the country. speechtext: Then, you give your answer in due course. I suggest it is time we reflected very seriously, not only that the people of Canada may know what are the facts but that we as the elected representatives may justify the great trust that they repose in us.

-is not quite accurate. Certainly if he wants to put himself up as an authority in respect of every problem that engages our attention, he has not commended himself to me as an authority, if that is the

The Budget-Mr. Richardson basis for his authority and prestige in respect of the matters with which he deals. I suggest on this occasion he was wrong.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
