subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would simply repeat the question asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). Is it not a fact that this 20 per cent deduction is permitted under the Canadian income tax law?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly, and I said so to the hon. member who left the chamber just a minute ago. Does the hon. member wish me to emphasize the point?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member a question. Would he admit that capital gains amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars are exempt from income tax in Canada?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer that question. It is quite irrelevant to the question I was discussing and by saying that I am not trying to dodge it. I was not in any way, nor were my hon. friend's two colleagues, discussing the question of capital gains. They were discussing the very simple question of the taxation of corporations and the dividend rebate which is allowed to shareholders, thousands of them throughout Canada. They receive a 20 per cent dividend rebate by way of reducing to the extent of one-fifth of the income which is charged to them as shareholders throughout the artificial entity, the corporation.
I have stated my case on that. I only make it in order that, while I myself as one member in this house who refrains, perhaps with not too much modesty but' enough for one of my profession, from discussing problems of wheat, mining and fishing about which I feel I know extremely little, I think it is also becoming for all of us at times to remember that there are people who have not only become the primary producers of the economic wealth of Canada but have through a process of law become corporations and kept a great deal of the trade and commerce of this country at a relatively high level. That is the whole point I wanted to bring to the attention of the house in answer to the hon. member for Nanaimo.
I come again to the fact that these people of Canada from whom we have to garner the revenue with which to pay all the bills, this revenue which parliament will disperse throughout the length and breadth of this country for the coming year, is coming from a narrower and narrower segment of society.

The older people continue to be a large group and the younger people are becoming a larger and larger group. We must remember that it is from these people that we get the ways and means whereby to discharge these duties and obligations of a collective society, not necessarily of the government or even of the members of parliament because we are only a small body called a government or a parliament. It is not from parliament or the government that these revenues come to pay our friends their old age pensions or the other pensions or to pay the younger people their supplementary grants for education; this revenue comes from the taxpayers of Canada. So long as we frequently come back and reflect on that, the better we will discharge the obligations imposed upon each of us.
In closing, may I point out a strange phenomenom. If you go back to 1867 and, for example, take 10 year periods, 1877, 1887, 1897, 1907, 1917, 1927, 1937, 1947, and this year 1957-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and 1967 to come, you will find that the budgets presented by every one of those ministers of finance, the illustrious predecessors of the present minister, with the exception of 1887 and 1917, have been presented by a minister who was a member of this particular party.
( Translation):

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget just brought down by the government has been coldly received by the Canadian public. While the government lavished advice on the Canadian people on ways to prevent inflation, the government itself failed to take any really practical steps along those lines. Government restrictions will seriously hinder residential construction: they will embarrass municipalities and school boards and strangle small industries.
All economists agree that, in times of inflation, more money must be put in the hands of the consumer, and that attempts must be made to lower the cost of living. Therefore family allowances should have been doubled, at least, to increase the buying power of the consumer. Actually this would only have brought back the value of the family allowances to the level of 1945. A government which boasts of a fantastic increase in Canadian prosperity, which spends untold millions every year and even manages at that to accumulate huge surpluses, suddenly feels incapable of paying family allowances on the scale of 1945 when its revenue was considerably less.
The insistence of our requests, which merely echoed the thousands of requests

made by the families of our various constituencies, has no doubt constrained it to yield something, but the benefits offered are so measly that we are tempted to refer to them as "electoral allowances". The government, in all its own expenses, is prodigal to an alarming degree but where the family is concerned, it is downright miserly. Averaged out over all the families already in receipt of family allowances, this increase comes to only $1.40 per month per family. There are two and one half million families at present in receipt of family allowances and they are to be voted $3,660,000 per month. Moreover, according to the new conditions, not all children will benefit from this $1.00 a month increase but only those in the 1 to 6 year group and those in the 10 to 12 year group. This means that the children aged 6, 7, 8, 9, 13, 14, 15 and 16 will receive absolutely nothing more. As the increase will take effect only on September 1st, chances are that most families will realize only after the elections how few children will be entitled to it.
The same niggardliness was shown towards our old people, $6 a month being granted when it should have been $15. The 55-year old man can no longer find employment in industry today because he is too close to retirement. The cruel and inhuman rule of retirement at 65 throws him out of the labour market. At 70 he will have to be content with a miserly $46 a month to clothe and feed himself, to find lodgings and to live. Such is the gratitude of the state towards its older citizens who have made our country what it is today and who have sown the harvest of millions of dollars which are being spent under their noses while they are given a few crumbs. The poor old man whose pension is inadequate will at least find some solace in the thought that he is getting a little less because his government has decided to give the pension to all those who have reached the required age, and that he is sharing it generously with those who do not need it.
Why does not the government stop its extravagant expenditures, in order to reduce the income tax paid by workers in the low income brackets and by the corporations? That would be an efficient way of reducing the cost of living and of further increasing the purchasing power of the consumer. Just look around everywhere federal money is being spent and you will be impressed by the liberality with which use is made of the taxpayer's money, whereas the taxpayer would soon be called a prodigal son if he acted the same way.
The Budget-Mr. Girard
There is however a field where civil servants suddenly become thrifty. That is the field of unemployment insurance. In that field, the iron rule is applied and people are driven from pillar to post and treated as poor relatives by those who administer the worker's money. Because of a few hundred lazy people, who want to live off this fund accumulated by the workers, the others are shifted back and forth to the point of bewilderment. Some civil servants, themselves victims of the complexities of a law capable of many interpretations, too easily become repeating machines for which true human problems are dealt with in legal terms and are classified by numbers. Under the law as its stands, a specialized worker may very often get what he is looking for, but the unfortunate labourer has to accept any work anywhere, at the risk of being deprived indefinitely of unemployment insurance benefits.
I take this opportunity to ask the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to cover the staff of our hospitals and educational institutions. Those people suffier just as much as industrial workers from unemployment. These exceptions are discriminatory and impossible to explain. I make this request on behalf of 6,000 employees of the aluminum union of my constituency who urged me to do so as they are concerned, and rightly so, with the situation of their fellow-workers in other fields. They have thus given an example of solidarity of which they can be proud.
I also wish to say a few words about the agricultural problems which have been omitted from the budget. I read in the press that potato growers of New Brunswick are planning a march on parliament to ask of the government that it finally put a stop to the flow of American agricultural products flooding our markets. The potato growers of my own riding would surely like to endorse those representations, if they could only hope that the government would at last think of agricultural producers other than the wheat growers.
Recently a member complained in the house that American turkeys in Canadian packings were being imported into this country. As far as the Right Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is concerned, this seems to be normal.
We have the same problem for cheese imports from New Zealand. In a country with too much wheat, livestock producers are crushed by the prices of feeds while they continue to suffer from uncontrolled fluctuations in the price of their products.
2942	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Girard
When will the little farmer be free from the unemployment insurance red tape? If some farmers cannot live on their land and have to take jobs off the farm, this is a definite proof that they are entitled to unemployment insurance. To say that they are not eligible for unemployment benefits because they live on a farm is to make them the victims of a cruel injustice. The entitlement to benefits should not be determined by the area of a farm, but according to the income it brings to the owner.
Mr. Speaker, again this year I introduced a bill that I had submitted to the house last year, one that would grant a certain preference to bilingual applicants in civil service examinations. I would like to say a few words on this matter while we are discussing the budget.
The hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) has given me the assurance that something would be done in line with the purposes of this bill, but since the promises of the hon. minister have not yet begun to materialize, I come back to that subject, always confident that the hon. minister will finally give in.
When answering my question in this respect while the estimates were being discussed last year, the hon. Secretary of State even went so far as to congratulate me on my humble case for bilingualism. In the light of this encouragement, I dare bring the matter up again, not to annoy the government but in the hope of finding a solution to this unthinkable anomaly whereby, after 75 years of confederation, the public service has not yet found a way to determine whether a candidate is bilingual or not in a bilingual country.
Even though, to all appearances, my bill was quietly killed, as some newspapers put it, because an ominous silence has followed the encouraging words of the minister, I believe that the debate has served a useful purpose. That is why I would like to quote a statement of the Secretary of State as the starting point for a new discussion.
I quote from Hansard of July 4 last, page 4 of the English translation:
Just as my hon. friend, I am convinced that bilingualism is making notable headway in this country. I agree with him that there is still room for improvement. Some time ago, the hon. member introduced in the house a bill containing certain suggestions. At that time, I opposed the bill as it was drafted but I clearly stated that I approved it in principle. By what means the suggestions made in that bill could be implemented remains to be seen. Personally, I believe, as my hon. friend, that bilingual employees should receive not a preferential but a different treatment, on account of that extra qualification, and that they

should therefore be given preference over any nonbilingual candidate to a civil service position. Some system might be devised to achieve that end. Following the introduction of my hon. friend's bill,-indeed I had done so before that-I discussed the matter at some length with representatives of the civil service commission and I asked them to suggest as soon as possible some amendments to the civil service regulations so as to do justice to the employees concerned.
So the minister himself recognizes that there is a serious deficiency, that bilingualism is not yet recognized by the civil service as an extra qualification. Moreover the federal civil service has not yet had proper regard for the spirit of confederation; it has failed to realize that Canada is a country with two races and two cultures. Its practice of bilingualism has gone no further than a concession to a single province and to certain French groups in particular. It does not look upon it as a prerogative of the whole Canadian nation.
Bilingual in the province of Quebec and unbilingual in the remainder of the country, this has been the separatist formula applied to date. Yet, whenever isolationism is mentioned, we Quebecers are accused of fostering it.
In my opinion, there are two kinds of bilingualism in Canada.
First, there is practical bilingualism, the one which is required for contacts with the French or English group, and which becomes a useful concession for the smooth operation of the civil service. By nature, it is inevitably restricted to the province of Quebec and a few important French groups. But there is, to my mind, another bilingualism, whose letters of nobility come out of the very spirit of our constitution and which ensures an exchange between the two ethnic groups who are the distinctive feature, not only of Quebec Canadians, but of Canada as a whole.
It is for this latter form of bilingualism we must fight, since French culture is not only the heritage of the people of Quebec but also of all Canadians, from Halifax to Vancouver.
That is why I am opposed to the mentality which is evidenced even in the speech of the minister who only consents to bilingualism in so far as it ensures proper relations with the French-speaking group.
We must not learn French and English only because this would be a useful accomplishment, but we must learn the two official languages to be more truly Canadian, to be more apt to possess this double culture which is the main national resource of Canada and the basic element of its national character. To say that for an English-speaking Canadian

from Vancouver a knowledge of French is not necessary is to give French-Canadians the right to make similar claims. This means the destruction of the bicultural character of the nation. The civil servants are the trustees of the constitution and they must remain so wherever they may live. I do not hold that bilingualism should be extended to every Canadian without exception. I am of those who believe it necessary to have an adequate knowledge of one's own mother tongue before learning another. But for those whose role has consequences on the life of the Canadian nation, bilingualism is indispensable to a fair and universal representation of this nation of ours, with its dual mentality.
These people see in bilingualism not only a sign of competence, nor a concession made to good understanding but a sign that our nation has no business being anything but a country with two cultures.
When, Mr. Speaker, will we cease to be content with words, promises, or high sounding principles? When will we take practical steps to show how sincere these fine words can be?
When will the end come at last to the exploitation of popular feelings by resounding symbols outside the house, while the last positions of the French group in the constitution are being destroyed in parliament?
How can some people decently give recognition to the principle of bilingualism in fine speeches, and refuse to approve a bill which merely requests constitutional confirmation of that fine principle? The symphony of the pompous speeches on national unity has been so well orchestrated that national centralization can be substituted to them without any change in the music. To that are added some professions of good intentions and the trick is done. Our constitutional rights can be destroyed with impunity, approval of legislation aiming at bilingualism of cheques and civil servants can be refused consistently, there can even be intrusions in the sacred sanctuary of education, etc., and the people are completely hoodwinked.
On January 23rd last, the federation of all St. John the Baptist societies of Quebec submitted to the Secretary of State an eloquent brief supporting the principle of my bill on bilingualism. As reported in the newspapers, the Secretary of State replied that he would seriously consider the matter. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), in his speech, admitted that there is inflation; he admitted that there was an increase in the cost of production. The rapid increase in the cost of living is having a very serious effect on the Canadian economy, and on the way of life of almost everyone of us.
The minister admits also that something must be done to stop this inflation, but, oddly enough, he gives us no recipe for its cure; he does not tell us how he is going to stop it. All he says is: "We are going to put a little pressure on here; we are going to make a little increase in the cost of borrowing money." The reverend brothers, because of

their charitable work, are obliged to extend their activities continually. As owners of a lot that has not been used so far but which was intended for the erection of a building necessary to the expansion of their institution, the reverend brothers, due to the expropriation imposed on them, have been forced to acquire an adjacent lot. This lot was sold to them by the reverend Jesuit fathers at a cost of $1,000 an acre, which is considerably more than the amount offered by the officers of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority as compensation for their own lot.
I might add that the sale carried out by the Jesuit Fathers to the Brothers of Christian Education took no account of the market value. Rather was this transaction carried out in a spirit of charity and conciliation. As it happens I do know that the Jesuit Fathers asked between $1,500 and $2,000 an arpent for the property they have at Laprairie. It might also be pointed out that the property purchased by the Brothers of Christian Education had no access to the highway, being situated in the rear of the parish cemetery and consequently could be of no conceivable use for any future buyer with the sole exception of the brothers who were the owners of the adjacent land.
I might also point out here the case of a land owner whose farm was situated within the limits of the town of Laprairie and who was offered approximately $600 an arpent. About a year ago this man sold two lots, with a total area less than one arpent, for $40,000. How can the owner accept the offers now being made?
Cases such as the one I have just mentioned are numerous. However, knowing the fairness which the officials of the seaway authority have shown in the transactions they have had to make with the expropriated owners of Caughnawaga, of Cote Sainte-Catherine and elsewhere, I have no doubt that the rights of the owners of the Laprairie area will also be respected.
I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, that a most brilliant future is in store for the south shore area and I wish to thank the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), who is now at his desk, about the construction of a new bridge between the island of Montreal and the south shore. This undertaking, which is to start soon, will help considerably towards the solution of traffic problems between the metropolis and the south shore.
I wish also to congratulate the Minister of Transport in connection with the improvements made to Victoria bridge.
